This document proposes best practices to minimize these information leaks when building heterogeneous transactions.

entries.title: BIP-0127
entries.body: Definition of a standard proof-of-reserves format based on intentionally invalid Bitcoin transactions. Currently at draft status, BIP-0127 allows custodians to prove cryptographically that they control certain UTXOs without having to move them. The proof transaction includes a first so-called “commitment” input (*commitment input*) whose `txid` is replaced by the SHA-256 hash of a proof message. It is this fictitious input that makes the transaction invalid and impossible to confirm on the blockchain. The other inputs are signed normally and correspond to the funds held. The transaction has a single output whose amount is equal to the sum of all the inputs, with no mining fees. BIP-0127 relies on the PSBT format of BIP-0174 to facilitate the construction of proofs with existing wallet infrastructure, and also defines a file format based on Protocol Buffers to group several proofs together with their associated metadata.

entries.title: BIP-0129
entries.body: Proposal defining the BSMS (*Bitcoin Secure Multisig Setup*) protocol, a standard for the secure setup of multisignature wallets between different hardware and software signers. The protocol uses an encryption scheme and token-based (*token*) coordination for the exchange of extended public keys and of the wallet configuration. It ensures that all cosigners agree on the same parameters (signature threshold, descriptor, derivation paths) before finalizing the creation of the wallet. BIP-0129 is adopted by several software products such as Nunchuk and Sparrow.

entries.title: BIP-0130
entries.body: Proposal adding the P2P message `sendheaders` to Bitcoin's network protocol. This message allows a node to ask its peer to announce new blocks to it directly via `headers` messages, rather than via `inv` messages followed by an explicit request. This mechanism reduces block propagation latency by eliminating an additional network round trip. The receiving node can thus begin validating the block header immediately after the announcement. BIP-0130 has been deployed and active on the Bitcoin network since 2016.

entries.title: BIP-0131
entries.body: Proposal for so-called “coalescing” transactions introducing *wildcard* inputs capable of automatically consuming all the UTXOs associated with the same address in a single operation. BIP-0131 aimed to simplify UTXO consolidation, but was rejected because of security issues and incompatibility with Bitcoin's existing transaction model.

entries.title: BIP-0132
entries.body: Proposal to create a committee in charge of accepting or rejecting BIPs according to a structured voting process with appointed members. BIP-0132 was firmly rejected by the Bitcoin community, as it was judged incompatible with the project's decentralized governance. This BIP was closed.

entries.title: BIP-0133
entries.body: Proposal adding the P2P message `feefilter` to Bitcoin's network protocol. This message allows a node to inform its peers of the minimum fee rate it accepts for transaction relay. When a node receives a `feefilter`, it refrains from sending transactions whose fees are below the indicated threshold. This mechanism reduces bandwidth consumption by avoiding the transmission of transactions that would be rejected anyway by the peer's mempool. BIP-0133 has been deployed and active on the Bitcoin network since version 0.13.0 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0134
entries.body: Proposal by Tom Zander (Bitcoin Classic) introducing a new flexible transaction format (“Flexible Transactions”) aiming to solve the transaction malleability problem. BIP-0134 was a direct competitor to SegWit, proposing a different approach based on tag encoding. It was never adopted, the network having activated SegWit (BIP-0141) instead.

entries.title: BIP-0135
entries.body: Proposal generalizing the *version bits* signaling mechanism defined in BIP-0009, with more flexibility in the soft fork activation parameters. BIP-0135 made it possible to configure the activation thresholds, signaling periods and expiration deadlines independently for each proposal. It was never deployed on Bitcoin.

entries.title: BIP-0136
entries.body: Proposal for a Bech32 encoding for transaction position references in the blockchain, combining the block height and the transaction index. BIP-0136 offers a compact and readable format to uniquely identify a confirmed transaction, with the advantages of Bech32: built-in error detection and case insensitivity. The goal was to replace the use of TXIDs for applications that needed it. This BIP has remained in draft since 2017.

entries.title: BIP-0137
entries.body: Proposes a standardized format for signing messages with Bitcoin private keys and their associated addresses, in order to prove possession of an address. This BIP aims to resolve the ambiguity related to the different types of Bitcoin addresses (P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH...) when signing a message. It introduces a method making it possible to explicitly distinguish these address formats through the signatures. These signatures are useful for various applications such as proof of funds, auditing, and other uses requiring authentication of an address via its private key. BIP-0322 has since introduced a new signature format that makes it possible to extend this standard and generalize it to any type of script.

entries.title: BIP-0140
entries.body: Proposal for normalized TXIDs excluding signature data from the calculation of the transaction identifier, in order to solve the malleability problem. BIP-0140 was an alternative approach to SegWit for obtaining stable transaction identifiers. It was closed because SegWit (BIP-0141) solved the malleability problem in a different way, while also bringing other advantages.

entries.title: BIP-0141
entries.body: Introduces the concept of segregated witness (*Segregated Witness*) which gives its name to the SegWit soft fork. BIP-0141 introduces into the Bitcoin protocol a major modification aiming to solve the transaction malleability problem. SegWit separates the witnesses (signature data) from the rest of the transaction data. This separation is achieved by inserting the witnesses into a distinct data structure, committed in a new Merkle tree, which is itself referenced in the block via the coinbase transaction, which makes SegWit compatible with older versions of the protocol.

entries.title: BIP-0142
entries.body: Proposal for an address format for SegWit based on the existing Base58Check encoding. BIP-0142 was superseded by Bech32 (BIP-0173), which offers better error detection, case insensitivity and optimized compatibility with QR codes. This address format was therefore never deployed on the Bitcoin network.

entries.title: BIP-0143
entries.body:
Introduces a new way of hashing the transaction for signature verification in post-SegWit scripts. The objective is to minimize redundant operations during verification and to include the value of the input UTXOs in the signature. This solves two major problems of the original transaction hashing algorithm: 
* The quadratic growth of data hashing with the number of signatures; 
* The lack of inclusion of the input value in the signature, which posed a risk for *hardware wallet*s, particularly regarding knowing the fees committed in the transaction.
Since the SegWit update, explained in BIP-0141, introduces a new form of transactions whose script will not be verified by old nodes, BIP-0143 takes the opportunity to solve this problem without requiring a *hard fork*. BIP-0143 is therefore part of the SegWit *soft fork*.

entries.title: BIP-0144
entries.body: Defines new network message formats and serializations for the broadcast of transactions and blocks that integrate segregated witness structures (SegWit). BIP-0144 notably establishes mechanisms allowing peers to signal their support for SegWit and to relay witness structures without compromising compatibility with nodes that are not up to date.

entries.title: BIP-0145
entries.body: Updates the JSON-RPC call `getblocktemplate` to integrate SegWit support, in accordance with BIP-0141. This update allows miners to build blocks taking into account the new “weight” measure of transactions and blocks introduced by SegWit, and other parameters such as the calculation of the sigops limit.

entries.title: BIP-0146
entries.body: Proposal aiming to fix two residual sources of signature malleability in Bitcoin transactions, after the adoption of strict DER encoding by BIP-0066. The first rule, “LOW_S”, requires that the S value of ECDSA signatures be in the lower half of the curve order, thus eliminating the malleability inherent to ECDSA signatures. The second rule, “NULLFAIL”, requires that any signature failing verification via `OP_CHECKSIG` or `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` be an empty byte array, thus preventing the replacement of invalid signatures with other invalid values. BIP-0146 has “closed” status, because these fixes were partially integrated into the standardness rules and into SegWit (BIP-0141), which solved the malleability problem more completely.

entries.title: BIP-0147
entries.body: Proposal included in the SegWit soft fork aimed at resolving a malleability vector related to the dummy element ("*dummy element*") consumed by the `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` operations. Because of a historical *off-by-one* bug (a unit offset error), these 2 opcodes remove one extra element from the stack in addition to their basic function. To avoid an error, it is therefore mandatory to include a dummy value at the start of the `scriptSig` in order to satisfy the removal and work around the bug. This value is useless, but it must be there for the script to be valid. BIP-0011, which introduced the P2MS standard, advised using a `OP_0` as the useless value. But this standard was not enforced at the consensus rule level, which means that any value could be placed there without invalidating the transaction. This is why `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` contained a malleability vector. BIP-0147 introduces a new consensus rule, known as `NULLDUMMY`, requiring that this dummy element be an empty byte array (`OP_0`). Any other value causes the script evaluation to fail immediately. This change applies to pre-SegWit scripts as well as P2WSH scripts and required a soft fork.

entries.title: BIP-0148
entries.body: Proposal introduced in March 2017 by a developer under the pseudonym Shaolin Fry. The goal of BIP-0148 was to force the activation of the SegWit upgrade on the Bitcoin protocol, in the face of stagnating signaling of this soft fork by miners via the BIP-0009 method. BIP-0148 suggested implementing a UASF (*User-Activated Soft Fork*) to forcibly activate SegWit by nodes on November 15, 2017, if miners had not locked in SegWit by August 1, 2017. Had the BIP-0148 UASF been adopted, Bitcoin network nodes would have rejected blocks that did not signal support for SegWit, thereby putting pressure on miners to adopt the upgrade. Although this historical BIP was ultimately not activated, it played a decisive role in the successful adoption of SegWit, by compelling miners to lock in the soft fork via BIP-0091. In the longer term, BIP-0148 set an important precedent, demonstrating the influence that users can exert through their full nodes on Bitcoin protocol governance decisions.

entries.title: BIP-0149
entries.body: Proposal by Shaolin Fry for a new deployment of SegWit (BIP-0141, BIP-0143 and BIP-0147) using the BIP-0008 activation method with `LOT=true`, if the initial deployment of SegWit via BIP-0009 failed to activate before November 15, 2017. Unlike the BIP-0009 method, where a failure to signal results in the activation being abandoned, BIP-0149 aimed to activate SegWit on July 4, 2018, whether or not miners had reached the 95% signaling threshold. During the eight-month period between November and July, nodes would have had the possibility of implementing BIP-0149, in order to ensure an activation of SegWit by the economic majority of the network if activation by miners did not occur (UASF). Once the first difficulty adjustment after July 4, 2018 was reached, activation would have moved to `LOCKED_IN`, and SegWit would have been activated at the following adjustment cycle. Unlike BIP-0148, which provided for a SegWit activation imposed by users or a majority of miners, BIP-0149 suggested a more gradual and measured activation method, although it remained resolutely offensive, according to the principles of BIP-0008. While BIP-0148 foreshadowed a conflict with a blockchain split, BIP-0149 ruled out this possibility, by accepting blocks that did not signal SegWit, barring a deliberate action by a miner (without incentive). BIP-0149 was therefore a less confrontational SegWit activation mechanism than BIP-0148, favoring a more gradual and less risky adoption for the system. Neither BIP-0148 nor BIP-0149 was ultimately implemented, SegWit having been activated through a MASF, notably under the impetus of BIP-0091.

entries.title: BIP-0150
entries.body: Proposes an authentication mechanism between peers on the Bitcoin network to strengthen security and guarantee node ownership. It allows node operators to restrict access to certain services or to grant data flow priorities only to specific peers, by mutually authenticating each other to avoid MITM attacks. This BIP was closed ("*Closed*"), but it served as a lesson for BIP-0324 (*P2P transport V2*), which is now implemented as an option in Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0151
entries.body: Proposes a protocol for encrypting P2P communications between peers on the Bitcoin network, in order to strengthen security and privacy. Its goal is notably to prevent traffic manipulation and mass surveillance attacks. Ultimately, BIP-0151 was replaced by BIP-0324 (*P2P transport V2*), which is now implemented as an option in Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0152
entries.body: "*Compact Block Relay*" proposal aimed at reducing the bandwidth required for transmitting blocks on the Bitcoin network. Adopted in November 2016 in version 0.13.0 of Bitcoin Core, this protocol makes it possible to communicate block information in a compact manner, based on the assumption that nodes already have a large part of the transactions of a recent block in their mempool. Rather than transmitting each transaction in full, which would be redundant, BIP-0152 proposes sending only short identifiers for the transactions already known to peers, accompanied by a few selected transactions (notably the coinbase transaction and those that the node is likely not to know). The node can then ask its peers for any missing transactions. Compact Block Relay thus reduces the amount of data exchanged during block propagation, which in turn reduces bandwidth spikes and improves the overall efficiency of the network.

entries.title: BIP-0154
entries.body: Proposal for a rate-limiting mechanism via cryptographic challenges imposed by peers on the Bitcoin P2P network. BIP-0154 aimed to mitigate denial-of-service attacks by requiring requesting nodes to solve a small proof-of-work challenge before obtaining a response. This approach was never deployed.

entries.title: BIP-0155
entries.body: Bitcoin improvement proposal introducing a new format for messages that relay addresses of nodes that accept incoming connections. This proposal makes it possible to support larger addresses, notably to facilitate the integration of network protocols such as Tor V3 or I2P, whose addresses are longer than those supported by the old `addr` message. This improvement is also known as `addrv2`.

entries.title: BIP-0156
entries.body:
Proposal, known as Dandelion, that aims to improve the privacy of transaction routing in the Bitcoin network to counter deanonymization. In Bitcoin's classic operation, transactions are immediately broadcast to multiple nodes. If an observer is able to see every transaction relayed by every node on the network, they can assume that the first node to send a transaction is also the originating node of that transaction, and therefore that it comes from the node operator. This phenomenon can potentially allow observers to link transactions, normally anonymous, with IP addresses. 

The goal of BIP-0156 is to address this problem. To do so, it introduces an additional phase in the broadcast that preserves anonymity before public propagation. Thus, Dandelion first uses a "stem" phase where the transaction is sent through a random path of nodes, before being broadcast to the entire network in the "fluff" phase. The stem and the fluff are references to the behavior of the transaction's propagation through the network, which resembles the shape of a dandelion ("*a dandelion*" in English).

This routing method blurs the trail leading to the source node, making it difficult to trace a transaction through the network back to its origin. Dandelion therefore improves privacy by limiting adversaries' ability to deanonymize the network. This method is all the more effective when the transaction encounters, during the "stem" phase, a node that encrypts its network communications, as with Tor or *P2P Transport V2*. BIP-0156 was rejected and was not integrated into Bitcoin Core.

![Dandelion routing: stem phase (random walk) then fluff phase (star-shaped broadcast to the rest of the network).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bip-0156/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: BIP-0157
entries.body:
Proposal that defines the peer-to-peer protocol allowing light clients to download *compact block filters* from full nodes. This BIP introduces six new P2P messages: `getcfilters` and `cfilter` to request and receive filters, `getcfheaders` and `cfheaders` for filter headers, as well as `getcfcheckpt` and `cfcheckpt` for checkpoints spaced every 1,000 blocks.

BIP-0157 relies on a system of chained filter headers, similar to block headers. Each header is the double SHA-256 of the concatenation of the filter hash with the previous header, which allows the client to verify the authenticity of the filter chain. In case of conflict between peers, the client can download the full block, recompute the correct filter and identify the faulty peer.

This BIP requires BIP-0158, which specifies the construction of the filters themselves. Written by Olaoluwa Osuntokun, Alex Akselrod and Jim Posen, it is deployed in Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0158
entries.body:
Proposal that defines the structure and construction of the *compact block filters* used by the BIP-0157 protocol. The chosen format is based on *Golomb-Coded Sets* (GCS), a probabilistic structure more compact than the Bloom filters of BIP-0037.

The filter of type `basic` (`0x00`) contains, for each transaction in a block, the output scripts spent as inputs (except the coinbase) and the `scriptPubKey` of each output (except the `OP_RETURN`). The elements are hashed with SipHash (parameters `c = 2`, `d = 4`), the key being the first 16 bytes of the block hash. The hashed values are mapped into the range `[0, N \times M)`, sorted, then the successive differences are compressed by Golomb-Rice coding.

The chosen parameters are `P = 19` and `M = 784\,931`, optimized to minimize overall bandwidth by taking into account both the size of the filters and the number of blocks downloaded because of false positives. This BIP also introduces the service bit `NODE_COMPACT_FILTERS` (`1 << 6`). It was written by Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod.

entries.title: BIP-0159
entries.body: Proposal defining the service bit `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` (bit 10) for pruned nodes of the Bitcoin network. This bit indicates that a node is able to serve at least the last 288 blocks of the blockchain (about 2 days), even without having the full history. Before this BIP, pruned nodes could not signal their partial serving capability, which excluded them from block relay. BIP-0159 thus allows pruned nodes to actively participate in the propagation of recent blocks, improving the decentralization of the network without requiring storage of the entire chain.

entries.title: BIP-0171
entries.body: Definition of a standard API format for Bitcoin exchange rate data, allowing applications to query different price providers in a uniform and interoperable way. BIP-0171 specified the REST *endpoints*, the JSON response formats and the supported currency pairs, aiming to standardize access to market data. This proposal was closed, as data providers developed their own APIs without adopting a common standard.

entries.title: BIP-0172
entries.body: Proposal to officially define the satoshi (sat) as the standard subunit of Bitcoin and to promote its use in user interfaces. BIP-0172 aims to clarify the denomination by establishing that 1 bitcoin = 100,000,000 satoshis, and recommends displaying amounts in satoshis for small values, in order to avoid confusion related to decimal numbers.

entries.title: BIP-0173
BIP-0174
entries.body:
Defines the PSBT (*Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction*) format, a standard for exchanging unfinalized Bitcoin transactions between different actors such as software wallets, hardware wallets or multisig coordinators. The PSBT makes it possible to separate the steps of creating, updating, signing and finalizing a transaction. The protocol defines six distinct roles: the *Creator* creates the base transaction, the *Updater* adds the necessary information (UTXO, scripts), the *Signer* applies their signature, the *Combiner* merges the partial signatures, the *Finalizer* builds the final unlocking script, and the *Extractor* produces the transaction ready to be broadcast.

This format is essential for multisigs, hardware wallets, coinjoins, and any other workflow where signing is not done on the same device as the construction of the transaction.

entries.title: BIP-0175
entries.body: Description of the Pay-to-Contract (P2C) protocol allowing a contract to be committed into a public key via a cryptographic tweak. The payer modifies the recipient's public key by incorporating the hash of a contract into it, creating a new key that can only be spent by the recipient. This mechanism makes it possible to prove that a payment is linked to a specific contract without revealing the contract on the blockchain.

entries.title: BIP-0176
entries.body: Proposal to use the "bit" (100 satoshis, or one millionth of a bitcoin) as a standard denomination in user interfaces. BIP-0176 argues that the bit offers a good compromise between precision and readability for common amounts. This proposal competes with the movement toward the satoshi as the main reference unit, the latter gaining more traction in the ecosystem.

entries.title: BIP-0177
entries.body:
Proposal to redefine Bitcoin's base unit so that "1 bitcoin" corresponds to the current satoshi, eliminating decimals entirely. Under this new system, the current value of 1 BTC would become 100,000,000 of the new base unit. BIP-0177 aims to simplify the user experience by removing the confusion related to decimal fractions, which is particularly problematic for new users.

This change has been adopted by some applications, notably Bitkit, the wallet developed by Synonym, whose CEO, John Carvalho, is also the author of BIP-0177. In practice, however, the vast majority of wallet software for now keeps the standard of 1 bitcoin = 100,000,000 satoshis.

entries.title: BIP-0178
entries.body: Proposal for an extension of the WIF (Wallet Import Format) with an additional version byte indicating the type of script associated with the private key. BIP-0178 would make it possible to automatically distinguish whether a key is intended to be used with P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH or another type of script, thus avoiding errors when importing keys between wallets.

entries.title: BIP-0179
entries.body: Informational document proposing to replace the term "address" with "invoice" (or "*Bitcoin Invoice Address*") to designate payment reception identifiers in Bitcoin. BIP-0179 starts from the observation that the word "address" suggests permanent information (like a postal or email address), whereas Bitcoin addresses are designed for single use. The term "invoice" is proposed to better reflect this ephemeral nature and the link to a specific transaction. The permitted variants are "*Bitcoin Invoice Address*", "*Bitcoin Invoice*", "*Invoice Address*" and "*Invoice*", the suffix "*Address*" being tolerated as a transitional measure.

entries.title: BIP-0180
entries.body: Proposal for a fraud proof format for blocks exceeding the maximum allowed size or weight. BIP-0180 would allow light nodes to verify that a block respects the size and weight limits without having to download it entirely, by receiving a compact proof of violation. This approach aimed to strengthen the security of light clients. The proposal was closed.

entries.title: BIP-0197
entries.body: Proposal of HTLCCs (*Hashed Time-Locked Collateral Contracts*), an extension of HTLCs (*Hashed Time-Locked Contracts*) adding a collateral mechanism. BIP-0197 is designed to create debt agreements between two parties (a borrower and a lender), where bitcoin collateral is locked in a P2SH to guarantee a loan whose principal is denominated on another blockchain. In case of non-repayment, the collateral can be liquidated via an atomic swap or seized according to predefined conditions.

entries.title: BIP-0199
entries.body: Formalization of the construction of HTLCs (*Hashed Time-Locked Contracts*) in on-chain Bitcoin transactions. BIP-0199 describes the standard mechanism used for *atomic swaps* and Lightning payment channels: a *hashlock* combined with a *timelock* allowing conditional refunds. The recipient must reveal a secret (the hash preimage) before the deadline expires to claim the funds; otherwise, the sender can recover them.

entries.title: BIP-0300
entries.body:
Proposal by Paul Sztorc and CryptAxe defining the “*Hashrate Escrows*” mechanism (escrow by hashrate), which is the first technical building block of drivechains.

This BIP makes it possible to create sidechains whose two-way peg with Bitcoin is managed directly by miners, without relying on a federation of signers. The bitcoins sent to a sidechain are locked in a special output using `OP_DRIVECHAIN` (a redefinition of `OP_NOP5`). To withdraw funds to the main chain, a “*withdrawal bundle*” is proposed and then submitted to a miner vote spanning 26,300 blocks (about 6 months). Each miner can, block by block, vote in favor of a bundle, abstain, or trigger an alarm that reduces the score of all bundles. The withdrawal is executed only if the bundle reaches 13,150 votes in favor, which is about 50% of the hashrate over the period. This slowness is deliberate: it makes any theft attempt publicly visible for months, giving the community time to react.

BIP-0300 defines six consensus messages (M1 to M6) covering the proposal and activation of new sidechains, deposits and withdrawals.

This BIP has been the subject of significant debate: its supporters see it as a way to add features (privacy, smart contracts, scalability) on sidechains without modifying the base layer; its critics raise questions about the security model, since a 51% attack sustained for long enough could allow the theft of all of a sidechain's funds, and about a risk of mining centralization. BIP-0300 is therefore still in draft.

entries.title: BIP-0301
entries.body: Proposal by Paul Sztorc and CryptAxe defining “*Blind Merged Mining*” (BMM), a blind merged mining mechanism for drivechains. BMM allows Bitcoin miners to collect sidechain transaction fees in BTC on Bitcoin, without needing to run the software of each sidechain. BIP-0301 complements BIP-0300 to form the complete technical basis of drivechains.

entries.title: BIP-0310
entries.body: Proposal of extensions to the Stratum protocol used for communication between individual miners (the hashers) and mining pools. BIP-0310 introduces a generic feature negotiation mechanism via a new `mining.configure` message, which allows the miner and the server to agree on the supported extensions. The main extension specified is *version rolling*, which allows miners to modify certain bits of the `nVersion` field of the block header. The BIP also defines other extensions such as minimum difficulty and `subscribe-extranonce`. It is a conceptual predecessor of Stratum V2, which took up and built on these improvements by adding encryption of communications and transaction selection by the hashers.

entries.title: BIP-0320
entries.body: Proposal to reserve certain bits of the `nVersion` field of block headers for general-purpose use, separate from the soft fork signaling mechanism defined by BIP-0009. The main motivation of BIP-0320 is to allow the use of Overt ASICBoost in a clean way: this mining optimization technique requires modifying the block's version bits, which can interfere with soft fork signaling. By reserving dedicated bits, miners can use ASICBoost without ambiguity with activation mechanisms.

entries.title: BIP-0321
entries.body: Proposal updating the `bitcoin:` URI scheme defined by BIP-0021 to support SegWit addresses in bech32 and bech32m format. The original BIP-0021 was designed for Base58 addresses, which are case-sensitive. Since bech32 addresses are case-insensitive, BIP-0321 adapts the specification to allow their correct use in URIs, notably in QR codes where uppercase encoding is more efficient. This BIP ensures the compatibility of the Bitcoin URI scheme with modern address formats.

entries.title: BIP-0322
entries.body: Proposes a new standard to replace BIP-0137 for signing messages with Bitcoin private keys and their associated addresses, in order to prove ownership of an address. These signatures are useful for various applications such as proof of funds, auditing, and other uses requiring authentication of an address via its private key. Compared to BIP-0137, BIP-0322 extends the message signing standard beyond classic addresses, using a script-based approach. It allows wallet software to sign a message for any script they could unlock in order to spend bitcoins. To do this, the method consists of signing a text by producing a signature for a virtual Bitcoin transaction. For traditional P2PKH addresses, BIP-0322 remains compatible with the traditional signature format.

entries.title: BIP-0324
entries.body: Introduces a new version of the Bitcoin P2P transport protocol incorporating opportunistic encryption to improve the privacy and security of communications between nodes. The V2 P2P transport of BIP-0324 was included as an option (disabled by default) in version 26.0 of Bitcoin Core, released in December 2023. It can be enabled with the `v2transport=1` option in the configuration file. This improvement replaces BIP-0151.

entries.title: BIP-0325
entries.body: Proposal defining Signets, test networks for Bitcoin in which block production is controlled by a set of authorized signers, in addition to proof of work. Unlike the classic testnet, where anyone can mine and cause unpredictable reorganizations, blocks on Signet must contain a valid signature issued by designated keys. This makes the network stable, predictable and suited to application development and testing. The default signet is maintained by Kalle Alm and AJ Towns. It is possible to create custom signets with your own signing keys.

entries.title: BIP-0326
entries.body: Improvement proposal aimed at developers of Bitcoin wallet software supporting Taproot transactions. Its main goal is to strengthen the privacy of second-layer protocols that might use PTLCs (*Point Time Locked Contracts*), such as CoinSwap, the Lightning Network or DLCs (*Discreet Log Contracts*). To do this, this proposal aims to create plausible deniability by automatically setting the `nSequence` field of Taproot transactions in the same way the `nLocktime` field was set in other types of transactions in order to discourage *fee sniping* attacks. In other words, BIP-0326 asks wallet software to use the `nSequence` field rather than the `nLocktime` field to prevent *fee sniping* attacks, in order to offer increased privacy for all *off-chain* protocols using this field in a similar way. Thus, a Taproot transaction with a specific value in the `nSequence` field could be either an ordinary wallet spend, all things considered, or a settlement transaction of a second-layer protocol with a timelock, making these two cases indistinguishable. If this improvement proposal were widely applied by Bitcoin wallet software developers, it would greatly improve the privacy and fungibility of Bitcoin as a whole.

entries.title: BIP-0327
entries.body: Defines MuSig2, a multi-signature scheme in which *n* participants jointly produce a single Schnorr signature, indistinguishable *on-chain* from a classic individual signature. The protocol works in two rounds: an exchange of public *nonces*, then the generation of partial signatures which are combined into a final signature. Key aggregation is non-interactive: the aggregated public key can be computed by anyone from the individual public keys. MuSig2 thus enables an *n-of-n* *multisig* that appears as a single-key spend on the blockchain, which improves privacy and reduces transaction fees.

entries.title: BIP-0328
entries.body: Defines how to construct a synthetic BIP-0032 extended public key (xpub) from a MuSig2 aggregated public key (BIP-0327), and how to use it for child key derivation. Rather than requiring each participant to derive their individual keys before aggregating them at each level, BIP-0328 makes it possible to derive non-hardened child keys directly from a single synthetic xpub built on the aggregated key. This xpub uses a fixed, standardized chain code. This mechanism considerably simplifies the generation of receiving addresses in MuSig2 multisig wallets, by reducing the storage and computation required. When signing, participants must compute the corresponding BIP-0032 derivation tweaks and provide them in the MuSig2 session context.

entries.title: BIP-0329
entries.body: Proposal defining a standard JSON Lines format for exporting and importing wallet labels. This format covers labels for transactions, addresses, extended public keys and UTXOs. The goal is to allow users to migrate their labeling data between different wallet software without loss of information. BIP-0329 meets a practical need, since labeling transactions and addresses is essential for accounting and for users' privacy.

entries.title: BIP-0330
entries.body: Proposal known as “*Erlay*” which aims to optimize the propagation of unconfirmed transactions in the Bitcoin network. Currently, transactions are broadcast to all of a node's peers, which causes redundancy and excessive bandwidth use. BIP-0330 proposes to limit this broadcast to 8 peers by default, then to use a reconciliation mechanism to efficiently share the missing transactions. Erlay reduces bandwidth consumption by about 40%. It also avoids a linear increase in bandwidth consumption with the number of peers connected to the node.

entries.title: BIP-0331
entries.body: Proposal (draft) describing a P2P protocol for relaying packages of related transactions (*ancestor packages*). This BIP makes it possible to relay a low-fee parent transaction together with its higher-fee child transaction, thus making the CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*) mechanism effective at the network relay level. Without this protocol, a parent transaction whose fees are below the mempool minimum cannot be propagated, even if a child transaction is ready to compensate. BIP-0331 solves this problem by allowing nodes to evaluate the fee rate of the whole package rather than of each transaction individually.

entries.title: BIP-0337
entries.body: Proposal of a compression format for Bitcoin transactions, significantly reducing their size by omitting data that is redundant or deducible from context.

entries.title: BIP-0338
entries.body: Proposal of a P2P message `disabletx` allowing a node to indicate to its peers that it does not wish to receive relayed transactions on that connection. BIP-0338 targeted connections dedicated solely to block relay, thus reducing bandwidth and attack surface. This proposal was closed, as the feature was integrated differently into Bitcoin Core's network protocol.

entries.title: BIP-0339
entries.body: Proposal modifying transaction relay to use the `wtxid` (*witness transaction identifier*) instead of the classic `txid` when announcing and requesting transactions between peers. Before this BIP, a malicious peer could send invalid witnesses (*witnesses*) for a valid `txid`, thus wasting the receiving node's bandwidth. By using the `wtxid`, which incorporates SegWit witness data in its computation, each witness variant has a unique identifier, which prevents this class of denial-of-service attacks. Nodes signal their support via the `wtxidrelay` message exchanged during the version handshake.

entries.title: BIP-0340
entries.body: Defines the Schnorr signature scheme for Bitcoin's secp256k1 curve, activated with SegWit v1 (Taproot) in November 2021. Compared to ECDSA, Schnorr signatures offer several advantages: they are mathematically simpler, have a formal security proof, and natively allow key aggregation (MuSig2), batch verification and more compact multi-signatures. BIP-0340 uses 64-byte signatures (without DER encoding) and 32-byte *x-only* public keys, which reduces the size of on-chain data.

entries.title: BIP-0341
entries.body:
Defines the spending rules of SegWit version 1, commonly called “Taproot”. This BIP introduces two distinct spending paths: the *key-path*, which allows spending with a simple Schnorr signature, and the *script-path*, which allows revealing and executing a script from a Merkle tree (MAST). Taproot outputs use “tweaked” public keys that combine an internal key with the root of the MAST tree.

The advantage of this structure is that all Taproot outputs look identical on-chain (a simple 32-byte public key), which considerably improves user privacy. BIP-0341 was activated at block 709,632 in November 2021 via the Speedy Trial method.

entries.title: BIP-0342
entries.body: Defines Tapscript, the script language used for spends by script path (*script-path*) in Taproot (BIP-0341). Tapscript brings several changes compared to traditional Bitcoin Script. It replaces `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` with `OP_CHECKSIGADD`, a new opcode that facilitates batch verification of Schnorr signatures. BIP-0342 also introduces the `OP_SUCCESS` opcodes, which reserve ranges of opcodes for future protocol extensions without requiring a complex soft fork. Signature validation relies on the Schnorr scheme defined in BIP-0340. In addition, Tapscript removes the 10,000-byte per-script limit and the limit of 201 non-push opcodes that applied to Legacy scripts, thus offering more flexibility to developers.

entries.title: BIP-0343
entries.body: Specifies an alternative activation mechanism for the Taproot soft fork, based on BIP-0008 with the `LOT=true` parameter (mandatory activation). This BIP, proposed by Shinobius and Michael Folkson, was designed in parallel with the “Speedy Trial” deployed in Bitcoin Core, to ensure that miners could not block indefinitely the activation of a soft fork with overwhelming community consensus. The signaling period began at block 681,408 with a 90% threshold, and provided for mandatory signaling before block 760,032 if lock-in had not been reached. In practice, Taproot was locked in via Bitcoin Core's Speedy Trial at block 687,285 in June 2021 and activated in November, making BIP-0343 obsolete before its mandatory signaling phase became necessary.

entries.title: BIP-0345
entries.body: Proposal to add two opcodes, `OP_VAULT` and `OP_VAULT_RECOVER`, making it possible to create native “*vaults*” on Bitcoin. A vault is a security mechanism that imposes a waiting period when withdrawing funds: during this period, the owner can cancel the transaction and redirect the funds to a predefined recovery address. This system protects against theft by offering a window to react even if the main keys are compromised. Proposed by James O'Beirne, BIP-0345 was closed in favor of `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (BIP-0443).

entries.title: BIP-0346
entries.body: Proposes adding the opcode `OP_TXHASH` for Tapscript, which places on the stack the hash of certain selected fields of the current transaction. The choice of fields to include in the hash is determined by a *TxFieldSelector* parameter which makes it possible to specify precisely which parts of the transaction (inputs, outputs, amounts, sequences...) must be covered. Combined with `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` (BIP-0348), `OP_TXHASH` would allow a flexible form of transaction introspection and covenants, without requiring a dedicated opcode for each use case. Proposed by Steven Roose.

entries.title: BIP-0347
entries.body: Proposal to re-enable the opcode `OP_CAT` in Tapscript only. `OP_CAT` concatenates the top two stack elements into one (that is, it puts them end to end), with a maximum size of 520 bytes for the result. This opcode was originally present in Bitcoin, but was disabled by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2010 as a precaution, because of potential denial-of-service risks related to the exponential growth of data on the stack. Re-enabling it in Tapscript would make it possible to build covenants, Merkle trees verifiable in Script, quantum-resistant Lamport signature schemes, and many other cryptographic primitives. BIP-0347, proposed by Ethan Heilman and Armin Sabouri, is one of the most debated soft fork proposals since the activation of Taproot, because of the power and versatility that this simple opcode could offer.

entries.title: BIP-0348
entries.body: Proposes adding the opcode `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` for Tapscript, replacing `OP_SUCCESS204`. Unlike `OP_CHECKSIG`, which verifies a signature against the hash of the current transaction, this opcode makes it possible to verify a Schnorr signature (BIP-0340) on an arbitrary message supplied on the stack. It consumes three elements: a 32-byte public key, a message and a signature. The BIP deliberately does not define a VERIFY variant, for the sake of simplicity. Combined with `OP_TXHASH` (BIP-0346), it allows a fully generalized signature hash construction, paving the way for transaction introspection, delegation of spending rights, and the setup of Lightning Symmetry channels (LN-Symmetry / Eltoo). Proposed by Brandon Black and Jeremy Rubin, its status is “Draft”.

entries.title: BIP-0349
entries.body:
Proposal by Brandon Black and Jeremy Rubin introducing the opcode `OP_INTERNALKEY` in Tapscript. This opcode replaces `OP_SUCCESS203` (`0xcb`) and places the 32-byte *x-only* representation of the Taproot internal key (*internal key*) directly on the stack when a script is executed. Currently, a tapscript that needs to reference the internal key must include it explicitly in its data, which consumes an extra 8 vBytes on-chain. `OP_INTERNALKEY` eliminates this redundancy.

Beyond this space saving, the opcode opens up an important use case: “*re-keying*” while preserving the Merkle tree. When the internal key of a Taproot output is changed (for example, to add or remove a participant), the scripts in the tree's leaves that hardcode a reference to this key become inconsistent. With `OP_INTERNALKEY`, the leaves re-key automatically, because the opcode always returns the current internal key.

entries.title: BIP-0350
entries.body: Introduces Bech32m, a variant of the Bech32 address format (BIP-0173) that fixes a weakness in error detection for SegWit v1 and higher addresses. The original Bech32 format had a flaw: the insertion or deletion of “q” characters just before a final “p” character was not always detected by the checksum. Bech32m solves this problem by modifying the final constant of the *checksum*. SegWit v0 addresses (starting with `bc1q`) keep the original Bech32 format, while v1 and higher addresses (such as `bc1p` for Taproot) use Bech32m.

entries.title: BIP-0351
entries.body: Proposal for a private payment protocol using a payment code published by the recipient on the network. The payer derives a unique address for the recipient without prior interaction, using an encrypted notification transaction. BIP-0351 is an alternative approach to *silent payments* (BIP-0352), with different tradeoffs: it requires an *on-chain* notification transaction, but offers broader compatibility with existing wallets. Both proposals aim to eliminate address reuse while preserving the recipient's privacy.

entries.title: BIP-0352
entries.body:
Improvement proposal by Josibake and Ruben Somsen that introduces Silent Payments, a method for using static Bitcoin addresses to receive payments without producing address reuse, without interaction and without any visible on-chain link between the different payments. This technique eliminates the need to generate a new fresh receiving address for each transaction, which avoids the usual interactions in Bitcoin where the recipient must provide a new address to the payer.

In this system, the payer uses the recipient's public key and their own private key to generate a fresh address for each payment. Only the recipient, thanks to their private key, can compute the private key corresponding to this address. ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*), a cryptographic key exchange algorithm, is used to establish a shared secret that is then used to derive the receiving address and the private key (on the recipient's side only). To identify the Silent Payments intended for them, recipients must scan the blockchain and examine every transaction that matches the Silent Payments criteria. Unlike BIP-0047, which uses a notification transaction to establish the payment channel, Silent Payments remove this step, which saves one transaction. However, the tradeoff is that the recipient must scan all potential transactions to determine, by applying ECDH, whether they are addressed to them.

entries.title: BIP-0353
entries.body:
Bitcoin improvement proposal that defines a DNS-based resolution system for human-readable payment addresses. BIP-0353 makes it possible to associate an identifier in the format `utilisateur@domaine.com` with Bitcoin payment instructions, by storing this information in DNS TXT records, secured by DNSSEC.

Concretely, when a wallet receives an address such as `satoshi@example.com`, it makes a DNS query to:

```
satoshi.user._bitcoin-payment.example.com
```

This allows it to retrieve a payment URI in BIP-0021 format. This URI can contain an *on-chain* address, a BOLT-12 *offer* or instructions for *silent payments*, which makes the mechanism compatible with different payment protocols.

The main advantage is the user experience: addresses become memorable and reusable, without sacrificing privacy since the underlying protocols (BOLT-12, *silent payments*...) generate unique addresses/*invoices* for each payment. BIP-0353 was proposed by Matt Corallo and Bastien Teinturier in 2024.

entries.title: BIP-0360
entries.body: Proposes a new output type called “Pay-to-Merkle-Root” (P2MR), via a soft fork. P2MR works similarly to P2TR (Taproot, BIP-0341), but removes the key-path spend (*key-path spend*). This change is mainly intended to protect funds against long-term attacks by quantum computers, which could use Shor's algorithm (or another, still unknown algorithm) to derive private keys from public keys exposed on the blockchain. By removing the internal public key from the output, P2MR prevents this exposure and allows Tapscript scripts to be used in a way that is resistant to long-term quantum attacks.

entries.title: BIP-0370
entries.body: Defines the second version of the PSBT format (BIP-0174). Unlike version 0, where the unsigned transaction was fixed from creation, PSBT v2 allows interactive modification of the transaction before signing: participants can add or remove inputs and outputs collaboratively.

entries.title: BIP-0371
entries.body: Adds Taproot-specific fields to the PSBT format (BIP-0174). These fields include the internal key (*internal key*), the Merkle path (*Merkle path*) of the scripts, Schnorr signatures, and the Taproot script leaves (*tap leaf scripts*). This extension is necessary so that hardware wallets and multisig coordinators can properly construct, verify and sign Taproot transactions via the PSBT format.

entries.title: BIP-0372
entries.body: Addition of PSBT fields (BIP-0174) dedicated to *pay-to-contract* tweaks. BIP-0372 allows signers to know that a public key has been modified by a P2C tweak and to sign the transaction correctly, taking this modification into account.

entries.title: BIP-0373
entries.body: Adds MuSig2-specific fields (BIP-0327) to the PSBT format to enable collaborative signing via *hardware wallets* and coordinators. These fields include the participants' public keys, the public *nonces* and the partial signatures. BIP-0373 thus makes it possible to coordinate the two-round MuSig2 protocol through the exchange of PSBT files, without the different signers needing to interact directly with each other.

entries.title: BIP-0374
entries.body: Defines a discrete logarithm equality proof protocol (*DLEQ proof*) for the secp256k1 curve. This cryptographic mechanism would make it possible to prove that two points on the elliptic curve share the same secret scalar, without revealing the value of that scalar.

entries.title: BIP-0375
entries.body: Defines the PSBT fields needed to send Silent Payments (BIP-0352). This BIP includes each signer's ECDH *shares* as well as the DLEQ proofs (BIP-0374) attesting to the correctness of the computations. BIP-0375 allows several signers in a multisig context to collaborate to compute the Silent Payments output addresses through the exchange of PSBT files, without each participant needing to reveal their private key to the others.

entries.title: BIP-0379
entries.body:
Proposal formalizing Miniscript, a structured representation of a subset of Bitcoin Script that allows analysis, composition and generic signing of spending conditions. Miniscript establishes a correspondence between Script opcodes and a system of composable types, in which spending conditions can be combined using logical operators (AND, OR, thresholds) with correctness guarantees.

This approach allows wallets to automatically determine the signature requirements for a given output, to precisely estimate transaction fees by computing the maximum witness size, and to verify that a spending policy is satisfiable. Miniscript was developed by Pieter Wuille, Andrew Poelstra and Sanket Kanjalkar.

entries.title: BIP-0380
entries.body: Improvement proposal that introduces a standard language for describing collections of output scripts (*output scripts*) of Bitcoin HD wallets. This language is called “*Output Script Descriptors*”. It aims to standardize the way output scripts are represented and managed, in order to make wallet backup, export and import easier. In addition to private data such as the recovery phrase, the *descriptors* provide all the information needed to recover the key pairs used in an HD wallet. BIP-0380 describes the general operation of *descriptors*, while BIP-0381, BIP-0382, BIP-0383, BIP-0384, BIP-0385 and BIP-0386 specify the expressions used. BIP-0380 was implemented along with all the other BIPs related to *descriptors* (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0381
entries.body: Introduces functions for descriptors, notably `pk(KEY)` (Pay-to-PubKey), `pkh(KEY)` (Pay-to-PubKey-Hash), and `sh(SCRIPT)` (Pay-to-Script-Hash). These functions standardize the way Legacy script types are described in descriptors. BIP-0381 was implemented along with all the other descriptor-related BIPs (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0382
entries.body: Introduces the functions `wpkh(KEY)` (*Pay-to-Witness-PubKey-Hash*) and `wsh(SCRIPT)` (*Pay-to-Witness-Script-Hash*) for *descriptors*. These functions standardize the way SegWit script types are described in *descriptors*. BIP-0382 was implemented along with all the other BIPs related to *descriptors* (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0383
entries.body: Introduces the functions `multi(NUM, KEY, ..., KEY)` and `sortedmulti(NUM, KEY, ..., KEY)` for descriptors. These functions make it possible to describe multisignature scripts in descriptors, with `sortedmulti` sorting the public keys in lexicographic order to ensure compatibility on import. BIP-0383 was implemented along with all the other descriptor-related BIPs (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0384
entries.body: Introduces the function `combo(KEY)` for descriptors. This function describes a set of possible output scripts for a given public key. It therefore makes it possible to cover several script types at the same time, notably P2PK, P2PKH, P2WPKH and P2SH-P2WPKH. If the given key is compressed, all 4 script types are tested, and if it is not, only the 2 Legacy script types are tested. The goal is to simplify the representation of keys in descriptors by providing a single method for generating different variants of output scripts built on the same public key. BIP-0384 was implemented along with all the other descriptor-related BIPs (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0385
entries.body: Introduces the descriptor functions `addr(ADDR)` and `raw(HEX)`. The function `addr(ADDR)` makes it possible to describe an output script using a receiving address, while the function `raw(HEX)` makes it possible to specify an output script using a raw hexadecimal representation of that script. BIP-0385 was implemented along with all the other descriptor-related BIPs (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0386
entries.body: Introduces descriptor functions for Taproot. It defines the functions `tr(KEY)` and `tr(KEY, TREE)` to find Taproot outputs, where `KEY` is the internal key and `TREE` is an optional tree of script paths. BIP-0386 was implemented in version 22.0 of Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: BIP-0387
entries.body: Proposal defining the output script descriptors `multi_a()` and `sortedmulti_a()` for multisig in Tapscript using the opcode `OP_CHECKSIGADD`. These descriptors are the equivalent of `multi()` and `sortedmulti()` used in traditional scripts, but adapted to Taproot script-path spending (*script-path spending*). The variant `sortedmulti_a()` sorts the public keys in lexicographic order to guarantee a deterministic result.

entries.title: BIP-0388
entries.body: Proposal defining “wallet policies” (*wallet policies*), a restricted subset of output script descriptors optimized for hardware wallets. Full descriptors can be arbitrarily complex and difficult to display on the limited screens of signing devices. BIP-0388 simplifies the format by separating the structure of the descriptor (the “template”) from the list of keys, while remaining expressive enough to cover common configurations: singlesig, multisig and MuSig2. This approach allows the user to visually verify the spending policy on the screen of their hardware wallet before signing a transaction.

entries.title: BIP-0389
entries.body: Proposal extending output script descriptors with multipath key expressions (*multipath key expressions*) using the syntax `<M;N>`. For example, `<0;1>` in a derivation path makes it possible to represent both receiving addresses (index 0) and change addresses (index 1) within a single descriptor. Without this extension, two separate descriptors would be needed for the same wallet. BIP-0389 thus simplifies wallet backup by reducing it to a single string containing all the information needed to reconstruct the addresses.

entries.title: BIP-0390
entries.body: Proposal defining the key expression `musig()` for output script descriptors. This expression makes it possible to represent a MuSig2 aggregate key within a descriptor, enabling the standardized description of a Taproot key-path spend (*key-path*) involving several signers. Without this expression, there was no standardized way to describe a MuSig2 multisig in descriptors.

entries.title: BIP-0431
entries.body:
Informational BIP that describes “*transaction pinning*” attacks, and proposes topological restrictions on transaction packages in the mempool in order to mitigate this type of attack. Pinning is a technique in which an attacker exploits the limitations of mempool policies to prevent the confirmation of a legitimate transaction, which is particularly problematic for upper-layer protocols such as Lightning.

BIP-0431 proposes limiting the structure of transaction packages: no multiple unconfirmed parents, restricted package size, and prohibition of certain complex topologies. These constraints make transaction replacement more predictable and reliable, thereby facilitating the operation of protocols that depend on the rapid confirmation of transactions.

entries.title: BIP-0433
entries.body: Informational BIP that defines a new standard output type called “Pay-to-Anchor” (P2A). It is a SegWit version 1 output using a 2-byte script (`OP_1 0x4e73`) that anyone can spend. This output type is specifically designed to serve as an anchor for the CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*) mechanism: any participant can create a child transaction spending this output to increase the effective fee rate of the parent transaction. P2A replaces Lightning-specific *anchor outputs* with a universal mechanism, usable by any protocol that requires a fee adjustment after the creation of a pre-signed transaction.

entries.title: BIP-0434
entries.body: Proposes a generic mechanism for feature negotiation between Bitcoin network peers when a connection is established. Currently, each new P2P protocol feature requires the addition of specific messages exchanged after the version handshake. BIP-0434 replaces this ad hoc approach with a unified system in which nodes announce the features they support through a standardized set of negotiation messages. This simplifies the implementation of new network features and reduces the complexity of the peer connection protocol.

entries.title: BIP-0443
entries.body: BIP written by Salvatore Ingala that proposes the addition of `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (CCV), a general-purpose opcode for implementing covenants on Bitcoin. CCV makes it possible to verify that a transaction output respects a contract defined by a combination of a hash and data embedded in the Taproot public key through the *tweaking* mechanism. Unlike previous proposals targeting a specific use case, CCV offers a flexible framework that can serve multiple constructions: vaults with a recovery mechanism, improved Lightning channels, payment pools, and other protocols requiring introspection of transaction outputs.

entries.title: BIRTH DATE
entries.body: Refers to the date on which a wallet was created. This information is important when restoring a wallet, because it lets the software know from which block it must start searching for the transactions associated with that wallet. By knowing the birth date, the software can efficiently synchronize and recover the transaction history without having to scan the entire blockchain from the Genesis block.

entries.title: BISQ
entries.body: Open source decentralized exchange (DEX) platform software that allows buying and selling bitcoins peer-to-peer, without a centralized intermediary or identity verification (KYC). Bisq works as a desktop application that connects to a P2P network over Tor. Each trade is secured by a security deposit system in bitcoins (2-of-2 multisig) and an arbitration process in case of dispute. Trades are made against fiat currencies (bank transfer, Revolut, etc.) or other cryptocurrencies. Bisq never holds users' funds and collects no personal data. The software is funded by an integrated DAO (decentralized autonomous organization) that uses the BSQ token for its governance.

entries.title: BIT
entries.body: The word "bit" is the contraction of the terms "binary" and "digit". In the context of computing and cryptology, a bit is the fundamental unit of digital information and represents the smallest possible quantity of information. A bit can only take two distinct values: `0` or `1`. These values are also called binary states and can represent various things, such as the answers `yes` or `no`, `true` or `false`, and `on` or `off`. Bits are the foundation of digital systems and are used to store and transmit information in computers and networks. The name "Bitcoin" probably comes from the concatenation of the term "Bit", to evoke the electronic nature of the payment system, and the term "Coin", to evoke its monetary purpose.

entries.title: BIT - UNIT
entries.body: In the context of Bitcoin, the term "bit" is also used to designate a monetary subdivision of bitcoin. One bit equals 100 satoshis, which represent the smallest indivisible unit of bitcoin. Thus, one bitcoin equals 1,000,000 bits or 100,000,000 satoshis. However, the use of this term as a monetary subdivision is controversial. The majority of bitcoiners use either "sats" or "btc", but not "bit".

entries.title: BIT GOLD
entries.body: Decentralized digital currency system conceptualized by Nick Szabo in 1998 and publicly described in 2005. Bit gold was designed to generate and exchange a virtual resource called bit gold. This system did not rely on any physical asset, but aimed to create a form of unforgeable scarcity. The bit gold protocol relied on monetary creation by proof of work, where pieces of bit gold were created through the computing power of computers, thus forming a chain of proof of work. Each proof of work was timestamped and then added to a property registry. Verification and transfer of ownership of bit gold were carried out through a public registry, where users were identified by public keys. Bit gold remained a concept and was never implemented. This system is one of the precursors of Bitcoin along with b-money and RPoW, but Satoshi seemed not to know of its existence before the creation of Bitcoin. They mentioned it later on the website and on the Bitcoin forum.

entries.title: BITAXE
entries.body: Open source project of a miniature Bitcoin miner based on an ASIC chip. The Bitaxe is a small mining device designed to be accessible, inexpensive and entirely transparent in its design, with hardware schematics and firmware published as open source. It uses mining ASIC chips (taken from consumer machines such as Bitmain's Antminer series) soldered onto a compact, standalone printed circuit board, powered by a simple USB-C cable. The Bitaxe is mainly used for educational purposes or for "lottery mining" (solo mining in the hope of finding a block probabilistically), because its computing power remains very low compared to large industrial mining farms.

entries.title: BITBANANA
entries.body: BitBanana is an open source Android application for remotely managing a Lightning node from your phone. Born as a fork of the Zap Android wallet (created by Jack Mallers), the project was taken over and renamed by developer Michael Wünsch to pursue independent development. The application offers a complete interface to supervise and control your node: channel management, sending and receiving payments, viewing logs and routing statistics. BitBanana is compatible with LND, Core Lightning and Nostr Wallet Connect, which makes it a versatile tool for Lightning node operators.

entries.title: BITBOX
entries.body: Hardware wallet made by the Swiss company Shift Crypto. The current model, the BitBox02, exists in two versions: a multi-crypto edition and a Bitcoin-only edition whose firmware is strictly limited to Bitcoin, thereby reducing the attack surface. The device includes a secure element, open source firmware and a touch interface operated by sliding on the sides of the device.

entries.title: BITCOIN - CAPITAL B
BITCOIN - LOWERCASE B
entries.body: The bitcoin (written with a lowercase "b") refers to the monetary unit used for exchanges on the Bitcoin electronic cash system (with a capital "B"). The bitcoin is often abbreviated as "BTC" or "XBT" and serves as a medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account within the network. Each bitcoin is divisible into 100 million smaller units, called "satoshis" or "sats", in honor of its creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. Bitcoins are issued through the proof-of-work process (mining). The total number of bitcoins is limited to approximately 21 million.

entries.title: BITCOIN ATM
entries.body: Physical kiosk that allows buying or, in some cases, selling bitcoins in exchange for fiat currency (cash or bank card). Also called BTM (*Bitcoin Teller Machine*), this type of machine offers a direct access point to Bitcoin without going through an online exchange platform.

entries.title: BITCOIN BEACH
entries.body:
Community initiative launched in the village of El Zonte, on the Pacific coast of El Salvador, which transformed this small town into the first circular economy running on Bitcoin. The project was born in 2019 thanks to a donation from an anonymous bitcoiner, with the aim of proving that Bitcoin could concretely improve the daily lives of people excluded from the traditional banking system.

Bitcoin Beach allowed residents to pay their bills (water, electricity, phone), their groceries or even the hairdresser directly in bitcoins via the Lightning Network. The wallet developed for the project, initially called "Bitcoin Beach Wallet", was later renamed "Blink".

The El Zonte experiment played an important role in El Salvador's decision to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, making the country the first state to take this step. The model has since inspired similar initiatives in other countries, notably Bitcoin Jungle in Costa Rica.

entries.title: BITCOIN CLASSIC
entries.body: Protocol fork proposal launched in January 2016 following the abandonment of Bitcoin XT. It aimed to increase the block size limit from 1 MB to 2 MB with BIP-0109, an approach considered more moderate compared to Bitcoin XT, which proposed a much larger increase (8 MB + doubling every 2 years). This initiative was led by developers Gavin Andresen and Jeff Garzik, and had the backing of major companies in the ecosystem such as Coinbase. Bitcoin Classic appeared in a context of sharp intensification of the Blocksize War and was classed in the big blockers camp. Although Bitcoin Classic attracted the attention and support of many players in the sector, its activation mechanism, which required the support of 75% of miners, was controversial and ultimately contributed to its failure.

entries.title: BITCOIN CORE
entries.body:
Bitcoin Core is the reference *open-source* software for the Bitcoin system, and is the main implementation of the Bitcoin protocol to date. It is developed and maintained by a large group of volunteer contributors. Initially named "Bitcoin Qt", it is the third client in Bitcoin's history after Bitcoin, by Satoshi Nakamoto, and Bitcoind. It was developed from Satoshi's original code and introduced a graphical user interface. Moreover, even today, the graphical interface of Bitcoin Core is called `bitcoin-qt`. It has been shipped with `bitcoind` since version 0.5. The Bitcoin Core software serves several purposes. First, it acts as a full node client. Bitcoin Core also includes a wallet (*wallet*) for users who wish to store, manage and make transactions directly with Bitcoin Core.

![Official Bitcoin Core logo, the reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol maintained by volunteer contributors.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bitcoin-core/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: BITCOIN CORE GUI-QML
entries.body:
Project underway to create a Bitcoin wallet and node application built on Bitcoin Core, but with an intuitive graphical interface developed using QML (*Qt Modeling Language*). The goal of Bitcoin Core GUI-QML is to modernize the Bitcoin Core user interface to offer a simpler, smoother and more dynamic experience. 

The traditional Bitcoin Core interface is mainly developed in C++ with Qt Widgets, which is a system that produces very classic user interfaces. This new project now relies on QML, which is a declarative language used to design GUIs with animations, transitions and a more responsive and stylized interface. This will allow Core to move closer to modern application interfaces with rich interactions. The goal is for this software to be available on both PC and mobile.

entries.title: BITCOIN FOG
entries.body: Centralized mixing service that operated from 2011 to 2021. Bitcoin Fog offered users the ability to increase their privacy by mixing their bitcoins with those of other users, with the aim of dissociating the coins from their transaction history. Given its centralized nature, users had to trust the service operator not to misappropriate the funds and not to keep a record of the mixing operations.

entries.title: BITCOIN INQUISITION
entries.body: Software fork of Bitcoin Core that aims to test the integration of new Bitcoin improvement proposals in a controlled environment on test networks such as a Signet. It includes, for example, support for BIP-0118 (ANYPREVOUT) and BIP-0119 (CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY). The goal of Bitcoin Inquisition is to experiment, in order to gain a better understanding of the applications, advantages, risks and trade-offs associated with these changes. Bitcoin Inquisition is maintained by Anthony Towns.

entries.title: BITCOIN JESUS
entries.body: Nickname given to entrepreneur and investor Roger Ver, who was a promoter of Bitcoin from the early 2010s. This nickname was given to him because of his influential role in popularizing Bitcoin at its launch. He is also known for his support of the Bitcoin Cash (BCH) *hard fork*, which he considers more faithful to Bitcoin's original vision.

entries.title: BITCOIN KEEPER
entries.body: Open source Bitcoin wallet developed by BitHyve, specialized in multisig. The application allows creating multisignature vaults (*vaults*) by combining different hardware wallets and software keys. Bitcoin Keeper supports BIP-0085 for derivation of sub-wallets, purchasing bitcoins directly into cold storage, and automatic transfer to multisig vaults. It is available on mobile (iOS, Android) and on desktop.

entries.title: BITCOIN KNOTS
entries.body:
Minority implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. Bitcoin Knots is an alternative to the reference software Bitcoin Core, offering a few different rules and features, while remaining compatible with other nodes. Knots is developed and maintained by Luke Dashjr.

![Bitcoin Knots logo, a minority implementation alternative to Bitcoin Core, maintained by Luke Dashjr.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bitcoin-knots/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: BITCOIN MAGAZINE
entries.body: Publication founded in 2012 by Mihai Alisie and Vitalik Buterin (before the latter created Ethereum), dedicated to Bitcoin news and analysis. Bitcoin Magazine is one of the oldest media outlets specialized in the Bitcoin ecosystem. It offers articles, technical analyses, interviews and educational content covering all aspects of Bitcoin: protocol, economics, regulation, mining and development. The magazine exists as a website, a print publication and video content. Bitcoin Magazine also organizes the "Bitcoin Conference", one of the largest annual events of the Bitcoin community, which is held in the United States and brings together developers, entrepreneurs, investors and enthusiasts from around the world.

entries.title: BITCOIN OPTECH
entries.body: Non-profit organization that focuses on sharing technical information for businesses using Bitcoin. Bitcoin Optech offers a wide variety of technical resources on Bitcoin, notably an excellent weekly newsletter. This newsletter summarizes the most important discussions and the latest news concerning the development of Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. To subscribe to the newsletter, go to: [https://bitcoinops.org/en/newsletters/](https://bitcoinops.org/en/newsletters/).

entries.title: BITCOIN QT
entries.body:
Bitcoin QT is a Bitcoin client integrating a graphical interface, released in November 2011. It follows in the lineage of Satoshi's own client. In 2014, Bitcoin QT was renamed "Bitcoin Core". Today it is the reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. It has been shipped with `bitcoind` since version 0.5. Moreover, even today, the graphical interface of Bitcoin Core is called `bitcoin-qt` in reference to the software's origins.

*"QT" comes from the name of the library used for the graphical interface. The name "QT" is sometimes interpreted as a pun on the sound of the term "cute" ("mignon" in French).*

entries.title: BITCOIN TREASURY COMPANY
entries.body:
A publicly traded company that places bitcoin at the center of its treasury strategy, accumulating bitcoins on its balance sheet rather than holding its reserves in fiat currency or bonds. The goal is to protect against monetary debasement while offering shareholders indirect exposure to bitcoin through traditional shares.

MicroStrategy (now Strategy) popularized this model under the leadership of Michael Saylor starting in August 2020. The company finances its bitcoin acquisitions through the issuance of convertible debt and shares, which creates a leverage effect on the price of bitcoin. Several other companies have since adopted similar strategies, such as Metaplanet in Japan or Semler Scientific in the United States.

This model allows institutional investors who cannot hold bitcoin directly to gain access to it through a conventional stock market vehicle, but it also exposes shareholders to the risks of financial leverage and of the volatility of the underlying asset.

entries.title: BITCOIN UNLIMITED
entries.body: A Bitcoin protocol update proposal that appeared at the end of summer 2016, aiming to increase the block size flexibly via a hard fork. This fork was supported by the big blockers during the Blocksize War, with, notably, Roger Ver. Unlike Bitcoin Classic, Bitcoin Unlimited did not set an upper limit on block size, but allowed users to define their own parameters. These parameters included the maximum generation size, the excessive block size and the acceptance depth. However, Bitcoin Unlimited was criticized for its technical complexity and its security flaws. This update was ultimately never adopted.

entries.title: BITCOIN XT
entries.body: A Bitcoin fork launched in 2015 by the well-known developer Mike Hearn and supported by Gavin Andresen (former lead maintainer of Bitcoin following Satoshi's departure). Bitcoin XT was originally an implementation of the Bitcoin protocol compatible with Bitcoin Core. However, in August 2015, version 0.11A of Bitcoin XT adopted BIP-0101: a hard fork proposed to increase the block size limit from 1 MB to 8 MB, with a planned increase to double this size every two years until reaching a little over 8 GB per block in 2036. This proposal was one of the casus belli of the Blocksize War that took place between 2015 and 2017. It was supported by a large share of miners, and by influential companies such as BitPay, Blockchain.info and Circle. Ultimately, Bitcoin XT would not manage to obtain enough support from the community, and Mike Hearn would end up announcing his departure from the community and the sale of his bitcoins. He would express his disappointment in a blog post in which he would notably declare that Bitcoin had failed.

entries.title: BITCOIN-CLI
entries.body: `Bitcoin-cli`, an acronym for “*Bitcoin Command Line Interface*”, is a command-line interface designed to interact with a running instance of Bitcoin Core, in particular the daemon, `bitcoind`. It is a standalone program that gives the user a way to communicate and execute commands to control and query the state of the `bitcoind` instance. In addition to network management capabilities, such as monitoring transactions and blocks, `bitcoin-cli` also offers wallet functionality, allowing users to make Bitcoin transactions by sending and receiving funds.

entries.title: BITCOIN-DEV
entries.body:
An email mailing list dedicated to the development of the Bitcoin protocol. Bitcoin-dev was created by Jeff Garzik in 2011 and initially hosted on Sourceforge.net. The mailing list was later moved to the Linux Foundation, then to Open Source Lab, and finally, since February 2024, it has been hosted on Google Groups: https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev

This mailing list is a meeting point for developers and researchers involved in the evolution of Bitcoin. Discussions there are strictly technical or academic. It is notably here that drafts of BIPs (Bitcoin Improvement Proposals) must be sent, before possibly being integrated into the BIPs GitHub repository. Its moderators are currently Ruben Somsen, Bryan Bishop and Warren Togami.

Participation in this list is open to all contributors, but it is mainly aimed at those with technical expertise in the field of Bitcoin. If you wish to receive these exchanges by email, you can subscribe to this mailing list. If you would rather have a summary of these discussions, you can also subscribe to the Bitcoin Optech newsletter: https://bitcoinops.org/en/newsletters/

entries.title: BITCOIN.CONF
entries.body: A configuration file used to customize the operation of a Bitcoin node running the Bitcoin Core client. Located in the Bitcoin Core data directory, this text file allows node operators to specify various parameters and options that influence the node's behavior. Among the parameters that can be set in `bitcoin.conf` are items such as the size of the Mempool, restrictions on network connections, the minimum relay transaction fees, as well as other security and performance options.

entries.title: BITCOIND
entries.body: Acronym for “*Bitcoin Daemon*”. It is software that implements the Bitcoin protocol and allows users to run a node for remote procedure calls known as RPC (“*Remote Procedure Call*”). It is a command-line program (without a GUI) that serves as a communication interface with Bitcoin. In other words, it is a program that runs in the background with which the user can interact (daemon). `Bitcoind` was part of Satoshi Nakamoto's original client. Some consider it the second client in the history of Bitcoin, after Satoshi's first one, since version 0.2.6 of the software allows this execution as a daemon without a graphical interface. It was subsequently merged with Bitcoin QT in 2011, a client later renamed “Bitcoin Core”, in 2014. Today, `bitcoind` is therefore fully integrated into the Bitcoin Core client.

entries.title: BITCOIND.PID
entries.body: A file generated by the bitcoind software (Bitcoin Daemon) while it is running. This file contains the process identifier (PID) of the running bitcoind instance. It is used to track and manage the software's process, allowing other applications or scripts to easily identify it and interact with it if necessary.

entries.title: BITCOINJ
