entries.body: An open-source library that implements the Bitcoin protocol in Java, created by Mike Hearn in 2011. It is designed to operate in SPV (*Simplified Payment Verification*) mode: instead of downloading the entire blockchain, it retrieves only the block headers and uses Bloom filters to identify relevant transactions. This lightweight operation makes it suitable for mobile devices and resource-constrained environments. Bitcoinj has served as the basis for many projects, notably the Bitcoin Wallet app (which no longer exists), Bisq and RSK.

entries.title: BITCOINTALK
entries.body: An online forum dedicated to discussions about Bitcoin. Opened in November 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto, this forum takes over from the Bitcoin discussion space on sourceforge.net. It acquired its name during the migration from bitcoin.org to bitcointalk.org in August 2011. BitcoinTalk serves as a platform for the exchange of information, news, technical debates and analyses.

entries.title: BITKEY
entries.body: A hardware wallet (*hardware wallet*) developed by Block, Inc. (formerly Square), the company founded by Jack Dorsey. Launched in December 2023, Bitkey relies on a 2-of-3 multisignature architecture that distributes the keys between the physical device, a mobile application and an encrypted recovery server managed by Block. This design aims to simplify *self-custody* for non-technical users by eliminating the need to manage a recovery phrase oneself. The device comes in a compact form that includes a fingerprint sensor and communicates with the application via NFC.

entries.title: BITKIT
entries.body: A self-custodial mobile Bitcoin wallet (*self-custody*) developed by Synonym, which combines on-chain and Lightning Network payments in a single application. Bitkit offers two accounts: “Savings” (on-chain) and “Spending” (Lightning), as well as *coin control* and the purchase of gift cards via Bitrefill. The software is open source.

entries.title: BITMAIN
entries.body:
A Chinese company founded in 2013 by Jihan Wu and Micree Zhan, specializing in the design of ASIC chips dedicated to Bitcoin mining and the production of mining machines. Bitmain sells the Antminer range, which historically dominates the global mining hardware market in terms of market share. The company also founded AntPool in 2014, one of the largest mining pools, before separating from it in 2021 to refocus on chip design.

Bitmain has played a central role in the industrialization of Bitcoin mining by making ASICs accessible on a large scale. The company has nevertheless stirred controversy, notably over the secret use of AsicBoost (Covert AsicBoost) in its machines and its opposition to the SegWit soft fork during the block size conflict in 2017.

entries.title: BITREFILL
entries.body:
A no-KYC online service that allows you to buy gift cards, phone top-ups and subscriptions using bitcoins. Bitrefill is a gateway between the Bitcoin economy and the traditional economy: users can spend their bitcoins at hundreds of retailers (Amazon, Uber, Steam, etc.) without those retailers directly accepting bitcoin payments.

The service supports on-chain and Lightning Network payments, which allows near-instant transactions. Bitrefill is often used by bitcoiners who want to live as much as possible on BTC, while still accessing the goods and services of traditional commerce.

entries.title: BITVM
entries.body: A protocol introduced by Robin Linus in 2023, which aims to extend Bitcoin's application development capabilities. BitVM makes it possible to perform any computation in an arbitrary way and to use that computation to direct the committed bitcoins. The protocol consists of moving all computation off-chain while allowing the computation to be challenged on-chain if the other party claims a fraudulent result. BitVM thus gives Bitcoin a quasi Turing-complete computing capability, without requiring any change at the consensus level. BitVM reproduces the behavior of a `NAND` logic gate through the joint use of the opcodes `OP_BOOLAND` (which itself reproduces the behavior of a `AND` logic gate) and `OP_NOT` (which reproduces the behavior of a `NOT` logic gate). Indeed, this `NAND` logic gate can be chained to reproduce the behavior of all the other existing logic gates. This is what is called a “universal gate”. By extension, a series of `NAND` logic gates can therefore reproduce any computation circuit. The idea with BitVM is to store these series of `NAND` computations as leaves in the MAST of a Taproot transaction.

entries.title: BLIND ORACLE
entries.body:
A cryptographic protocol in which an oracle performs operations (signing, encryption) on a confidential message transmitted by a user, without being able to know its content. The user can then verify the validity of the result without having exposed the original message to the oracle. This mechanism generally relies on blind cryptography techniques (*blind cryptography*), such as blind signatures or commitment schemes.

In the context of Bitcoin, the concept of *blind oracle* is notably used in Blockstream's Jade *hardware wallet*. The wallet encrypts the recovery phrase locally and uses a remote oracle for PIN protection, without this oracle having access to the private keys or the recovery phrase. This approach constitutes a “virtual secure element” (*virtual secure element*) that aims to protect against physical attacks, without requiring a dedicated secure chip.

entries.title: BLINDED PATHS
entries.body:
A Lightning routing technique that hides part of the payment path in order to protect the recipient's identity. In classic routing (SPHINX), the sender builds the entire route and therefore knows the recipient's public key. With *blinded paths*, the recipient encrypts the last hops of the route through an ECDH key exchange: it derives a shared secret with each node of the hidden segment, generates blinded node identifiers and produces encrypted data allowing each relay to discover only the next hop. The sender sees the route only up to an *introduction point*, without knowing the nodes beyond it or the final recipient.

*Blinded paths* are specified in BOLT-04 and are an important element of BOLT-12 offers, where each invoice includes one or more blinded paths. They can also be used in BOLT-11 invoices via bLIP-0039. *Blinded paths* also make it possible to route payments through private channels without revealing them. The recipient can add dummy hops (*dummy hops*) to strengthen anonymity, because the sender cannot distinguish the real relays from the decoys.

entries.title: BLINK
entries.body: A custodial mobile Bitcoin wallet, formerly known as “Bitcoin Beach Wallet”. Developed by Galoy, it was originally created for the Bitcoin Beach community of El Zonte in El Salvador. It allows you to manage balances in BTC and USD (via Stablesats), and to send or receive Lightning and on-chain payments.

entries.title: BLIP
entries.body: Acronym for “*Bitcoin Lightning Improvement Proposal*”. bLIPs are standardization proposals for Lightning Network features that do not require universal adoption, unlike BOLTs. They serve to document application extensions, optional protocols or usage conventions between compatible implementations. The process of creating a bLIP follows a community review cycle: an author submits a draft to the dedicated GitHub repository, which is evaluated, then progresses from *Draft* status to *Proposed* and then *Active* depending on consensus and adoption. bLIPs complement BOLTs by offering a lighter and more flexible framework for proposing innovations without modifying the protocol's fundamental specifications.

entries.title: BLIP-0001
entries.body: The first bLIP, which establishes the process for creating and managing bLIPs (*Bitcoin Lightning Improvement Proposals*). It defines the lifecycle of a proposal: submission of a draft, review by the editors for technical soundness and formatting, then progression through the *Draft*, *Proposed* and *Final*/*Active* statuses. bLIP-0001 clarifies the distinction with BOLTs: bLIPs cover application features and non-universal extensions, while BOLTs remain reserved for protocol changes requiring adoption by all implementations.

entries.title: BLIP-0002
entries.body: A bLIP that establishes a value reservation registry to avoid conflicts between the different Lightning Network proposals. Without coordination, two bLIPs could use the same message identifier, the same *feature bit* or the same TLV type, causing network incompatibilities. bLIP-0002 centralizes reservations in four categories: *feature bits* (beyond 255), message types (range 32768-65535), TLV extension fields of existing BOLT messages (`init`, `payment_onion_payload`, `update_add_htlc`, `ping`) and onion message payloads. Each entry is linked to the bLIP that uses it.

entries.title: BLIP-0003
entries.body: A bLIP that formalizes the specification of *keysend*, a spontaneous payment mechanism on the Lightning Network. With *keysend*, the sender generates a random 32-byte preimage, includes it in a TLV record (type `5482373484`) of the onion packet and uses its SHA-256 hash as the payment hash. The recipient verifies the match between the preimage and the hash to validate the payment. *Keysend* should eventually be replaced by more complete mechanisms such as BOLT-12 offers.

entries.title: BLIP-0004
entries.body: A bLIP that proposes an experimental HTLC endorsement signaling mechanism (*endorsement*) to fight *channel jamming* attacks on the Lightning Network. Each HTLC carries a one-byte TLV field indicating whether it is endorsed (value 7) or not (value 0). Originating nodes mark as endorsed the payments they expect to succeed. Intermediate nodes propagate the positive signal if they are compatible, otherwise they forward the default value of zero. This mechanism is purely observational: the collected data is used to test reputation algorithms without affecting the actual routing of payments. The experiment is limited in time by an expiration date, after which nodes stop relaying the signal.

entries.title: BLIP-0010
entries.body:
A bLIP that standardizes the metadata format attached to Lightning payments in podcasting applications (*Podcasting 2.0*). It defines a JSON structure transmitted via a TLV record (type 7629169) accompanying each payment. This metadata identifies the podcast, the episode, the playback timestamp, the amount in millisatoshis, the sender's information and an optional message.

The system supports two types of payments: *streams* (automatic micropayments per minute of listening) and *boosts* (manual contributions that may include a message called a “*boostagram*”). This standardization allows any compatible wallet to send payments that any compatible podcast host can process uniformly.

entries.title: BLIP-0011
entries.body:
bLIP that defines *NameDesc*, a standardized format for structuring BOLT-11 invoice descriptions by embedding the recipient's name. The convention consists of prefixing the description with the merchant's or recipient's name, followed by a colon and two spaces (`: `), then the payment description.

Compatible wallets can thus extract and display the recipient's name separately. Non-compatible wallets simply display the full text as a regular description, which guarantees full backward compatibility. This convention solves the problem of transaction histories where only a technical identifier or a product name appears, with no clear identification of the merchant.

entries.title: BLIP-0017
entries.body: bLIP that specifies *hosted channels*, Lightning payment channels based on the client's trust in a host, with no on-chain anchoring. Unlike classic Lightning channels, which lock bitcoins in a funding transaction, hosted channels operate without a UTXO or any interaction with the blockchain. The channel state is signed by both parties via encrypted messages exchanged over the Lightning protocol, which prevents the host from unilaterally falsifying balances. The advantages include immediate receiving capacity and the absence of on-chain fees, but the client bears a counterparty risk because they cannot force the channel to close on the blockchain. This model sits between a classic custodial wallet and a classic Lightning channel.

entries.title: BLIP-0025
entries.body: bLIP that allows the second-to-last hop of a Lightning route to forward an HTLC of a lower amount than the one encoded in the onion packet. The relay node declares the additional fees it has deducted via a new TLV field called `extra_fee`. This mechanism is mainly designed for Lightning service providers (LSPs) that open *just-in-time* channels for new users. By deducting additional fees from the first payment received, the LSP can offset the on-chain cost of opening the channel. The recipient explicitly verifies the amount of fees deducted, which prevents any abuse by the intermediate node.

entries.title: BLIP-0032
entries.body:
bLIP that defines a private DNS resolution protocol via Lightning Network onion messages. It allows a node to resolve domain names into TXT records with DNSSEC proofs, without going through a public DNS server. The protocol introduces two onion message types: `dnssec_query` (resolution request) and `dnssec_proof` (response with cryptographic proof).

The main use case is resolving human-readable identifiers in the `utilisateur@domaine` format into payment instructions, integrating with BOLT-12 offers. The recipient publishes their payment instructions in a DNS TXT record, and the payer retrieves them via the Lightning network without exposing their request to the public DNS infrastructure, thus preserving their privacy.

entries.title: BLIP-0039
entries.body: bLIP that introduces a new tagged field `b` in BOLT-11 invoices to convey blinded payment paths (*blinded paths*). This extension makes it possible to use *route blinding* (originally designed for BOLT-12) directly in existing BOLT-11 invoices, improving the recipient's privacy before the full deployment of BOLT-12 offers.

entries.title: BLIP-0050
entries.body: bLIP that defines LSPS0, the standardized transport layer for communication between Lightning service providers (LSPs) and their clients. The protocol reuses existing BOLT-08 peer-to-peer connections and carries JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over them via a unique message identifier (`37913`). The LSP acts as the JSON-RPC server and the client as the client, with named parameters and potentially out-of-order responses. LSPS0 also defines the common encoding schemas for amounts, fees, signatures and addresses used by all the higher-level LSPS specifications (LSPS1 to LSPS5). This architectural choice avoids introducing external dependencies such as HTTP or gRPC.

entries.title: BLIP-0051
entries.body:
bLIP that defines LSPS1, a standardized API allowing Lightning wallets to buy payment channels from Lightning service providers (LSPs). The process takes place in three steps:
* the client queries the LSP's available options via `lsps1.get_info`,
* it creates an order with the desired parameters (capacity, duration, balance distribution) via `lsps1.create_order`,
* then it pays via a BOLT-11 invoice, a BOLT-12 offer or an on-chain payment.

The LSP then opens the requested channel. The specification supports public and private channels, zero-confirmation channels, and provides for an automatic refund if the opening fails. LSPS1 relies on the LSPS0 transport layer of bLIP-0050.

entries.title: BLIP-0052
entries.body: bLIP that defines LSPS2, a protocol for negotiating *just-in-time* (JIT) channels on the Lightning Network. It allows a client without an existing channel to receive an incoming payment: the LSP opens a channel on the fly when a payment arrives, and deducts the opening fees directly from the transferred amount.

entries.title: BLIP-0055
entries.body: bLIP that defines LSPS5, a *webhook* registration protocol allowing Lightning service providers (LSPs) to notify mobile clients when an event requires their attention. Mobile applications, suspended by the operating system when they are not active, lose their network connections and cannot receive payments or process expiring HTLCs. With LSPS5, the client registers a *webhook* URL with the LSP via three APIs: `lsps5.set_webhook`, `lsps5.list_webhooks` and `lsps5.remove_webhook`. The LSP contacts this *webhook* when an incoming payment arrives, when an HTLC is about to expire, when liquidity changes, or when an onion message needs to be delivered. Notifications are cryptographically signed by the LSP node's identity key.

entries.title: BLIXT WALLET
entries.body: *Open source* and *non-custodial* Lightning wallet for Android and iOS. Blixt embeds an LND node directly on the user's phone, thanks to Neutrino.

entries.title: BLK*.DAT
entries.body: Name of the files in Bitcoin Core that store the raw data of the blockchain's blocks. Each file is identified by a unique number in its name. Thus, blocks are recorded in chronological order, starting with the file blk00000.dat. When this file reaches its maximum capacity, the following blocks are recorded in blk00001.dat, then blk00002.dat, and so on. Each blk file has a maximum capacity of 128 mebibytes (MiB), which is equivalent to a little over 134 megabytes (MB). These files have been moved to the `/blocks` folder since version 0.8.0.

entries.title: BLKINDEX.DAT
entries.body: Name of the old file used in Bitcoin Core to store various information about the blockchain, replaced since version 0.8.0 by the files in chainstate/, blocks/index/ and blocks/rev*.dat.

entries.title: BLKTREE/
entries.body: Name of the old folder used in Bitcoin Core to catalog metadata about all the blocks. This folder was replaced by the `blocks/index/` folder in version `0.8.0`.

entries.title: BLOCK
BLOCK TEMPLATE
entries.body: Set of information provided by a Bitcoin node to mining software or a pool, containing the data needed to build a new candidate block. This structure includes the transactions selected for inclusion and the block header. Once the miner receives this information, they are able to start searching for a valid proof of work for the candidate block.

entries.title: BLOCK-RELAY-ONLY
entries.body:
Type of outbound connection in Bitcoin Core that only relays blocks, without exchanging transactions or node addresses. Since version 0.19.0 (November 2019), each node establishes 2 *block-relay-only* connections by default in addition to its 8 regular outbound connections.

These connections strengthen resistance to network partitioning and protection against eclipse attacks, because they increase the node's connectivity without revealing information about the network topology. Indeed, transactions and addresses are the main vectors through which an adversary can map the links between nodes. The absence of these exchanges makes *block-relay-only* connections invisible to a spy analyzing transaction propagation. They thus guarantee the node access to the legitimate blockchain even if all of its regular connections are compromised.

entries.title: BLOCKCHAIN
entries.body:
The blockchain is the name commonly given to the distributed timestamp server of the Bitcoin system. It is a chain of blocks. Each block is linked to the next by its cryptographic hash. To prevent double spending on Bitcoin without resorting to a central authority, each user must verify the non-existence of a transaction in the system. The only way to ensure the absence of a transaction is to be aware of all past Bitcoin transactions. To this end, transactions are timestamped within blocks, and each user has the entire blockchain.

*Following the many abusive marketing uses of the term “Blockchain”, notably in the late 2010s, many bitcoiners refuse to use this word. Some prefer to speak of “TimeChain” to refer to this concept. Others, referring to Satoshi Nakamoto's White Paper, speak of a “Proof-of-Work Chain”. In French, the English term “Blockchain” is generally accepted. One can also use the translation “chaîne de blocs”.*

entries.title: BLOCKS INDEX
entries.body: LevelDB data structure in Bitcoin Core that catalogs metadata about all the blocks. Each entry in this index provides details such as the block identifier, its height in the blockchain, the pointer to the block in the database, and other metadata. This indexing makes it possible to quickly find a block stored in memory.

entries.title: BLOCKS/REV*.DAT
entries.body: Name of the files in Bitcoin Core that store the information needed to possibly undo the changes made to the UTXO set by previously added blocks. Each file is identified by a unique number that is the same as that of the blk*.dat file it corresponds to. The rev*.dat files contain the undo data corresponding to the blocks stored in the blk*.dat files. This data is essentially a list of all the UTXOs spent as inputs in a block. These undo files allow the node to return to an earlier state in the event of a blockchain reorganization causing previously valid blocks to be abandoned.

entries.title: BLOCKSIGNERS
entries.body: In the context of Liquid (a Bitcoin sidechain), these are the entities responsible for building and validating blocks within this chain. Liquid uses a federation model where the *blocksigners*, selected from among the federation members, operate jointly to confirm transactions and create new blocks in order to form the sidechain's consensus. The *blocksigner* role is part of the functionaries in Liquid. The latter fulfill both this role and that of *watchmen* (guardians).

entries.title: BLOCKSIZE WAR
frenchAliases: GUERRE DE LA TAILLE DES BLOCS
entries.body:
Refers to a period of intense debate and conflict within the Bitcoin community between 2015 and 2017. This conflict was about whether the block size, limited to 1 megabyte since 2010 by Satoshi Nakamoto, should be increased to allow Bitcoin to process more transactions per block, and thus to scale (scalability).

The supporters of increasing the block size (known as the “*big blockers*”), led by early developers such as Jeff Garzik, Gavin Andresen and Mike Hearn, influential figures of the ecosystem such as Roger Ver, as well as a good share of the large mining companies, argued that this increase was necessary to reduce transaction fees and improve Bitcoin's scalability. They believed that this change could be made without consequences for the security of the system. On the other hand, the opponents of increasing the block size (known as the “*small blockers*”), mainly Bitcoin Core developers (Pieter Wuille, Peter Todd, Gregory Maxwell, Wladimir van der Laan, Luke Dashjr...) and part of the technical community, argued that this change would centralize the system because of the increased operational load on nodes. They put forward so-called second-layer scalability solutions, such as the Lightning Network, which would make it possible to handle a large quantity of transactions without having to modify the base protocol.

The debate over Bitcoin's approach to scalability has lasted since at least 2010, with the first attempt to increase the block size in October of that year via [a patch proposed by Jeff Garzik](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=1347.0). But it was during the period of the Blocksize War between 2015 and 2017 that the conflicts were most virulent, with several fork attempts being set up (Bitcoin XT, Bitcoin Classic, Bitcoin Unlimited, SegWit, SegWit2X and Bitcoin Cash), along with propaganda and influence strategies, as well as personal attacks. The abandonment of the SegWit2X hard fork on November 8, 2017, following the massive opposition of the community (“NO2X”), is often seen as the event marking the end of the Blocksize War, while the casus belli is sometimes considered to be the 0.11A update of the Bitcoin XT client, which implemented BIP-0101 on August 15, 2015. One could also consider that the end of the Blocksize War took place on August 24, 2017, the date on which the SegWit soft fork was activated following the campaign in favor of the “UASF”.

*In French, the “Blocksize War” is generally referred to as a proper noun. Some sometimes translate this term as “guerre des blocs” or “guerre de la taille des blocs”.*

entries.title: BLOCKSTREAM
entries.body: Company specializing in the development of solutions around Bitcoin. Blockstream is behind the Liquid sidechain, the Core Lightning implementation of the Lightning Network, and the Jade and Green wallets. It is also known for employing Bitcoin Core developers. The company Blockstream is currently led by the cypherpunk and cryptographer Adam Back, the inventor of Hashcash, the protocol that inspired the proof of work on Bitcoin.

entries.title: BLOOM FILTER
entries.body:
Probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is part of a set. Bloom Filters make it possible to quickly check membership without testing the entire data set. They are particularly useful in contexts where space and speed are critical, but where a low, controlled error rate is acceptable. Indeed, Bloom Filters do not produce false negatives, but they do produce a certain quantity of false positives. When an element is added to the filter, several hash functions generate positions in a bit array. To check membership, the same hash functions are used. If all the corresponding bits are set, the element is probably in the set, but with a risk of false positives. Bloom filters are widely used in the field of databases and networks. Google is notably known to use them for its distributed storage system for structured data *BigTable*. In the Bitcoin protocol, they are notably used for SPV wallets according to BIP-0037.

*When speaking specifically of the use of Bloom Filters in the context of Bitcoin transactions, the term “Transaction Bloom Filtering” is sometimes found.*

entries.title: BLUE WALLET
entries.body: *Open source* mobile Bitcoin wallet available on iOS and Android. The application makes it possible to create several wallets within the same interface, to manage PSBTs for use with *hardware wallets* and to import wallets as *watch-only*. BlueWallet can be connected to your own Bitcoin node and your own Electrum server for sovereign use. It also offers advanced features such as *coin control*, transaction replacement via RBF and fee customization.

entries.title: BOLT
entries.body: Acronym for “*Basis of Lightning Technology*”. It is a series of specifications intended to enable Lightning interoperability between the different implementations of this second-layer protocol (*LND*, *Core Lightning*, *Eclair*...). These specifications detail the rules and standards to be followed so that Lightning nodes form one and the same network.

entries.title: BOLT-00
entries.body: Introductory document and index of the BOLT (*Basis of Lightning Technology*) specifications. It presents an overview of how the Lightning Network works, as well as each BOLT.

entries.title: BOLT-01
entries.body: Specification that defines the base messaging protocol between Lightning nodes. It establishes the message format, their classification into five categories (setup, channel, commitment, routing and custom messages) and the fundamental data types. BOLT-01 introduces the TLV (*Type-Length-Value*) format, an extensible encoding that allows implementations to ignore unknown fields while maintaining compatibility. It also specifies the `init` message exchanged on connection between two peers to declare their features, the `error` and `warning` messages for error handling, and the `ping`/`pong` mechanism for keeping connections alive.

entries.title: BOLT-02
entries.body: Specification that defines the peer-to-peer protocol for managing Lightning channels. It covers the entire lifecycle of a channel: establishment (in the classic version with a single funder, and in version 2 with dual funding via interactive transaction construction), normal operation (adding and resolving HTLCs, updating commitment transactions) and cooperative closing. BOLT-02 also specifies the mechanisms for increasing fees via RBF, the quiescence (*quiescence*) of the channel for protocol updates, and the message retransmission protocol upon reconnection between peers.

entries.title: BOLT-03
entries.body: Specification that defines the exact formats of the Bitcoin transactions and scripts used in Lightning channels. It details the structure of the funding transaction (2-of-2 multisig P2WSH output), of the commitment transactions (*commitment transactions*) that represent the current state of the channel with their `to_local` and `to_remote` outputs, and of HTLC transactions. BOLT-03 also specifies fee calculation, dust (*dust*) limits, key derivation procedures and the expected transaction weights for a correct fee estimation.

entries.title: BOLT-04
entries.body:
Specification that defines the onion routing protocol of the Lightning Network. It describes the construction and processing of 1,366-byte encrypted packets containing an ephemeral key, nested routing instructions and an integrity HMAC. Each intermediate node sees only the next hop, without knowing the sender or the final recipient.

BOLT-04 also covers *route blinding*, which hides the identity of downstream nodes to protect the recipient's privacy, and the encrypted error return mechanism that allows the sender to identify which node failed.

entries.title: BOLT-05
entries.body: Specification that defines the behavior of Lightning nodes when a channel is closed on-chain. It covers three scenarios: cooperative closing, unilateral closing (publication of a commitment transaction) and revocation closing (fraud attempt). BOLT-05 details the resolution of each type of output (local, remote, anchor and HTLC outputs), the rules for monitoring the blockchain until all funds are irrevocably resolved (100 blocks deep), and the penalty transactions that make it possible to seize all of the channel's funds when an old revoked state is published. The specification also describes the fee bumping (*fee bumping*) mechanisms via anchor outputs.

entries.title: BOLT-07
entries.body:
Specification that defines the peer-to-peer discovery protocol of the Lightning network. It describes the `node_announcement` messages (by which nodes broadcast their identity and connection addresses), `channel_announcement` (which prove the existence of a channel) and `channel_update` (which publish the routing fees and expiry deltas of each channel).

BOLT-07 establishes the rules for staggered broadcasting of announcements (*gossip*), the mechanism for pruning obsolete channels or channels closed on-chain, and the query-based synchronization protocols that allow nodes to maintain a consistent view of the network topology.

entries.title: BOLT-08
entries.body: Specification that defines the encrypted and authenticated transport layer of the Lightning Network. It is based on the Noise protocol, where the initiator must know the responder's public key before connecting. The *handshake* takes place in three acts, at the end of which both peers share session keys.

entries.title: BOLT-09
entries.body: Specification that establishes the centralized registry of *feature bits* used in the Lightning Network to signal the features supported by each node. Features are announced by *flags* in the `init`, `node_announcement` and `channel_announcement` messages. Each feature uses a pair of bits: the even bit indicates mandatory support, the odd bit indicates optional support.

entries.title: BOLT-10
entries.body: Specification that defines a DNS-based Lightning node discovery mechanism. It allows a node starting up with no known contacts to find initial peers (*bootstrap*) by querying authoritative DNS servers (*seed nodes*). Queries support filters by address type (IPv4, IPv6), by specific node identifier and by desired number of results. The DNS servers return a random sample of healthy nodes, with IP addresses via `A`/`AAAA` records (standard port `9735`) and `SRV` records for non-standard ports.

entries.title: BOLT-11
entries.body: Specification that defines the encoding format of Lightning payment invoices (*payment requests*), designed to be compatible with QR codes. A BOLT-11 invoice is encoded in Bech32 and consists of three parts: a human-readable prefix indicating the network and an optional amount (with multipliers `m`, `u`, `n`, `p`), a data section containing a timestamp and tagged fields (*tagged fields*), and an ECDSA signature. The tagged fields carry the payment hash, the payment secret, the description, the expiry delay, routing hints for private channels and feature flags. BOLT-11 is gradually being complemented by BOLT-12, which brings reusable invoices and better privacy.

entries.title: BOLT-12
entries.body:
Specification that defines a Lightning payment negotiation protocol that is more flexible than BOLT-11. It introduces three concepts: *offers* (reusable payment templates that can be published via QR codes), *invoice requests* (invoice requests sent over the Lightning network in response to an offer), and the invoices themselves.

Unlike single-use BOLT-11 invoices, BOLT-12 *offers* can be reused indefinitely and remain stateless on the merchant side. The format replaces the *tagged fields* of BOLT-11 with a more extensible TLV (*Type-Length-Value*) encoding, while retaining a bech32-style encoding, supports selective disclosure of fields, allows cross-currency payments and improves privacy via *blinded paths* that hide the recipient's identity.

entries.title: BOLTZ
entries.body: *Open source* service for performing *submarine swaps* and *atomic swaps* in a *non-custodial* manner between on-chain Bitcoin, the Lightning Network and the Liquid network. Launched in 2019, Boltz uses HTLCs to ensure that exchanges take place in a *trustless* manner, without either party having to trust the other. The service is sometimes integrated directly into wallet applications, in order to make it possible to use Lightning without having a node, while remaining in *self-custody*.

entries.title: BORROMEAN RING SIGNATURES
entries.body:
Cryptographic ring signature protocol that allows a signer to prove that they hold a private key among a set of public keys, without revealing which one. The name refers to Borromean rings, a topological structure in which three rings are linked in such a way that removing any one of them frees the other two. This scheme was formalized by Gregory Maxwell and Andrew Poelstra in 2015.

In the context of Bitcoin, *Borromean ring signatures* were used on the Liquid network as the initial *rangeproofs* mechanism within *Confidential Transactions*. They made it possible to prove that a committed amount was within a valid range, without revealing its value. This role was subsequently taken over by *Bulletproofs*, which offer more compact proofs.

entries.title: BOS - BALANCE OF SATOSHIS
entries.body:
Command-line tool developed by Alex Bosworth to manage and optimize a Lightning node running LND. It is installed via npm (`npm install -g balanceofsatoshis`) and offers a set of commands accessible through the `bos` prefix to view balances, adjust routing fees, rebalance liquidity between channels, open or close channels, and monitor node activity.

Among its main features, `bos rebalance` makes it possible to move liquidity between channels via circular payments, `bos fees` to dynamically adjust outgoing fees with conditional formulas, and `bos accounting` to produce an accounting statement of transactions. The tool also offers a Telegram integration to receive notifications and interact with one's node remotely.

entries.title: BOSMINER
entries.body: *Open-source* mining software developed in Rust by Braiins as a more modern alternative to CGMiner. BOSminer is specifically designed for ASICs. Integrated into the Braiins OS ecosystem, it allows advanced management of ASICs, with features such as overclocking, detailed performance monitoring and Stratum V2 support.

entries.title: BOUNTY
entries.body: Reward offered for the completion of a specific task, often related to the improvement or security of a software project. Bounties are often used to encourage the discovery and fixing of vulnerabilities in software, to develop new features, or to solve complex problems. Participants, generally developers or researchers, receive a reward once their contributions have been verified and accepted. This incentive system helps speed up development and strengthen software security by mobilizing a wider community. Bounties are sometimes used by software in the context of Bitcoin.

entries.title: BPM - BITCOIN POOLED MINING
entries.body:
Another name given to the “SCORE BASED METHOD” for calculating miners' remuneration in the context of mining pools. It is a proportional reward method, but weighted by the time at which the share is submitted. BPM values shares according to the time elapsed since the start of the mining cycle. The later a share is submitted in the cycle, the higher its value. This method encourages miners to stay, because each time a miner stops mining, their score stagnates while that of the others increases ever more quickly.

“*Bitcoin Pooled Mining*” was also the name of Slush's mining pool in 2010, which is the origin of the remuneration calculation method of the same name.

entries.title: BRAIDPOOL
entries.body:
Proposal for a decentralized mining pool for Bitcoin, designed by Bob McElrath. Braidpool aims to solve the centralization problem of traditional mining pools, where the pool operator selects the transactions and controls block construction.

The protocol is based on a DAG (*Directed Acyclic Graph*) mined in parallel to the Bitcoin blockchain. The blocks of the DAG are “weak blocks”: valid Bitcoin blocks that do not satisfy the difficulty target of the main network, but only a reduced target specific to Braidpool. These weak blocks act as shares and make it possible to measure each miner's contribution. Unlike P2Pool, which uses a linear sharechain, the DAG structure better tolerates network latency and reduces the rate of stale (orphan) blocks.

Each miner builds their own block templates and chooses the transactions to include, which preserves the decentralization of Bitcoin's consensus. At the end of each difficulty adjustment period, rewards are distributed to miners via a multisig transaction that uses the FROST protocol. Braidpool is still under development and is not yet deployed in production.

entries.title: BRAIINS POOL
entries.body: Bitcoin mining pool operated by the Czech company Braiins. Created in 2010 by Marek Palatinus (“Slush”), it is the very first Bitcoin mining pool, and it mined its first block on December 16, 2010. Initially known as “Bitcoin.cz Mining Pool”, then “Slush Pool” from 2016, it was renamed “Braiins Pool” in 2022. Braiins is also behind the Stratum V2 protocol, a major update to the communication protocol between miners and pools, which improves security, reduces bandwidth and allows miners to select for themselves the transactions to include in blocks. The company also develops Braiins OS, an open source firmware for ASIC machines.

entries.title: BRAINWALLET
entries.body:
Bitcoin wallet backup method that consists of not keeping one's mnemonic phrase on any physical or digital medium, and memorizing it only in one's head. By extension, the term sometimes also refers to choosing the words of one's mnemonic phrase oneself (instead of generating it randomly) in order to memorize it more easily. In both cases, the objective is not to depend on any physical medium.

This approach is doubly dangerous. First, human memory is fallible: forgetting, an accident or a death results in a permanent loss of funds, and raises an obvious problem of succession and inheritance. Second, when the user chooses the words of their mnemonic phrase themselves, the entropy of the phrase is dramatically low. Human beings are incapable of producing true randomness: even a phrase that seems random follows predictable patterns (common words, quotes, song lyrics...). Attackers exploit these biases with dictionaries and brute force techniques, and many brainwallets have been emptied within seconds of their creation.

The only scenario where a brainwallet can be justified is that of an urgent escape (crossing a border, checkpoint...), where no physical medium can be carried without risk. But even in this case, less risky alternatives exist: physical concealment of the phrase, steganography, encryption...

entries.title: BRANCH - BITCOIN
entries.body: In the context of Bitcoin, a branch is a sequence of valid blocks in which each new block is linked to the previous one. The blockchain represents the branch that contains the most accumulated work, but competing branches may exist as a result of forks. Each branch shares at least one block in common with the main branch, namely the Genesis block. The part of the blocks specific to the branch is sometimes called the “segment”. When two competing branches are present, honest nodes synchronize on the one with the most accumulated work. A branch is sometimes described as “strong” if it has more accumulated work than another, and as “weak” otherwise.

entries.title: BRANCH - GIT
entries.body: In the context of Git, represents a split from the main workflow, allowing parallel development without affecting the main branch (generally named `master` or `main`). Branches allow modifications, testing and experimentation in an isolated environment, before their possible integration into the main project via a *merge*.

entries.title: BRANCH-AND-BOUND
entries.body:
Method used for coin selection in the Bitcoin Core wallet since version 0.17 and invented by Murch. BnB is a search to find a set of UTXOs that matches the exact amount of the outputs to be satisfied in a transaction, in order to minimize the change output and the associated fees. Its goal is to reduce a waste metric that takes into account both the immediate cost and the expected future costs for the change output. This method is more precise in terms of fees compared to earlier heuristics such as the *Knapsack Solver*. *Branch-and-Bound* is inspired by the problem-solving method of the same name, invented in 1960 by Ailsa Land and Alison Harcourt.

*This method is also sometimes called “Murch's Algorithm” in reference to its inventor.*

entries.title: BRC-20
entries.body: Standard enabling interaction with non-native tokens on Bitcoin, based on inscriptions of the Ordinals protocol. Created by Domo in March 2023, this experimental standard sparked strong speculative enthusiasm, leading to a historic rise in transaction fees in April and May 2023. BRC-20 tokens use Bitcoin to store and timestamp JSON functions managing these assets. The functions are `deploy` (token creation), `mint` (token minting) and `transfer` (token transfer). To run this protocol, people must maintain servers that keep track of all the functions. The BRC-20 standard is thus a very poorly optimized use of Bitcoin compared to other token creation protocols such as RGB.

entries.title: BREEZ
entries.body:
Non-custodial Lightning Network mobile wallet that lets users send and receive bitcoin payments almost instantly. Breez embeds a Lightning node directly on the user's device, giving them full control of their funds without relying on a trusted third party.

The application stands out for its simplified interface, which hides the technical complexity of the Lightning Network, notably the management of payment channels and liquidity. Breez also includes point-of-sale features, allowing small merchants to accept Lightning payments directly from their phones. The company also offers the Breez SDK, an open-source development kit that lets other applications integrate Lightning payments by building on the Greenlight implementation of Core Lightning. Breez supports the LNURL and Lightning Address protocols to simplify receiving payments.

entries.title: BROLLUPS
entries.body: Concept of a native rollup on Bitcoin proposed by Burak in June 2024. Unlike optimistic rollups or rollups based on zero-knowledge proofs, Brollups form a category of their own. They rely on the concept of VTXO (*Virtual UTXO*), which comes from the Ark protocol, and use them as a peg mechanism (*peg*). The principle consists of exchanging VTXOs for call data (*calldata*), accompanied by new VTXOs, through coinswaps. Brollups are run by an operator or a quorum of operators who provide liquidity to the protocol and advance the rollup's state by chaining Bitcoin transactions at regular intervals. The Bitcoin blockchain serves as the data availability layer, while transactions are executed on a dedicated virtual machine called the *Bitcoin Virtual Machine*. The peg is executable on-chain and can be redeemed unilaterally at any time. Brollups require no modification to the Bitcoin protocol and are not associated with any token.

entries.title: BSMS
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Bitcoin Secure Multisig Setup*". BSMS is a protocol standardized by BIP-0129 that makes it possible to create a multisignature wallet securely among several signers (*hardware wallets*, software), ensuring that all of them agree on the same configuration before using it.

The protocol works in two rounds of exchanges between a Coordinator and the Signers. In the first round, the Coordinator defines the multisig parameters (M-of-N threshold, script type) and optionally distributes an encryption token (`TOKEN`) to each signer. Each signer then provides their extended public key, accompanied by their derivation path and a signature proving that they control the corresponding private key. In the second round, the Coordinator gathers all the keys, generates a wallet descriptor (*output descriptor*) and redistributes it to each signer. Each signer verifies that their own key is indeed included and that the wallet's first address is correct, which serves as a checksum over the whole configuration.

Three encryption modes are possible for the exchanges: no encryption, standard encryption with a shared 64-bit token, or extended encryption with a unique 128-bit token per signer. The encryption uses AES-256-CTR with a key derived via PBKDF2. The BSMS protocol is notably implemented in Nunchuk, Sparrow and ColdCard.

entries.title: BSV - BITCOIN SATOSHI VISION
entries.body:
Cryptocurrency system resulting from a hard fork of Bitcoin Cash (BCH), itself a fork of Bitcoin (BTC). The Bitcoin SV fork took place on November 15, 2018 at block 556,766 because of disagreements within the Bitcoin Cash community, notably concerning block size and the supposed vision of Satoshi Nakamoto, the creator of Bitcoin. Two camps clashed: 
* The supporters of the "Bitcoin Cash ABC" fork, which became Bitcoin Cash (BCH). This group was notably backed by the well-known entrepreneur Roger Ver;
* The promoters of the "Bitcoin Cash Satoshi Vision" fork, which led to the creation of Bitcoin Satoshi Vision (BSV). This camp was backed, among others, by Craig Wright.

Bitcoin SV differs from Bitcoin Cash, and even more so from Bitcoin, by its considerably high block size limit. This feature aims to align with what its supporters consider to be Satoshi Nakamoto's original vision for Bitcoin.

![Bitcoin SV logo, a fork of Bitcoin Cash that appeared on November 15, 2018 at block 556,766 around Craig Wright.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bsv-bitcoin-satoshi-vision/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: BTC
entries.body:
Stock market or monetary symbol (*ticker*) used to represent one unit of bitcoin on exchange platforms. It is used to quickly identify bitcoin among other assets and currencies. One unit of bitcoin (1 BTC) is equal to 100,000,000 satoshis (or "sats").

*"BTC" is the historical symbol of bitcoin, but it does not comply with the ISO 4217 standard, which governs currency codes. Under this standard, "BT" is assigned to Bhutan, and currencies not backed by a state, such as bitcoin, should begin with an "X". This is why some organizations use the symbol "XBT" for bitcoin. Although "XBT" is not yet officially recognized by the ISO 4217 standard, it nonetheless meets its criteria.*

entries.title: BTCD - BTC SUITE
entries.body: Minority implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. BTCD is an alternative to the majority software Bitcoin Core (notably Bitcoind). Unlike Bitcoin Core, which is developed in C++, BTCD is written in Go (golang). Its goal is to follow the consensus rules established by Bitcoin Core to ensure compatibility with the other nodes of the network. BTCD is developed as part of the BTC Suite project.

entries.title: BTCMAP
entries.body:
Open-source interactive map that lists businesses and services accepting bitcoin around the world. BTCMap relies on OpenStreetMap data and allows anyone to report or update the points of sale that accept bitcoin payments, whether on-chain or via the Lightning Network.

The tool is accessible through a website and allows searching for businesses by geographic location or by category (restaurants, hotels, shops). BTCMap helps make the ecosystem of merchants who accept bitcoin visible. Each point of sale can be verified by the community, and the information is timestamped to indicate the date of the last verification.

entries.title: BTCPAY SERVER
entries.body:
Open-source payment processor that allows merchants and users to accept bitcoin payments without depending on a third party to process transactions. Launched in 2017, BTCPay Server offers a bitcoin payment integration solution for e-commerce sites, with advanced features such as *hardware wallet* support, invoicing and accounting tools, as well as compatibility with the Lightning Network. Its development was initiated by Nicolas Dorier, in reaction to the actions of BitPay which, according to him, had misled its users by pushing them toward the adoption of SegWit2x, which the company wrongly considered to be the "real" Bitcoin. This opposition crystallized in a now-famous tweet by Nicolas Dorier in August 2017:

> "_This is lies, my trust in you is broken, I will make you obsolete_".

entries.title: BTG - BITCOIN GOLD
entries.body:
Cryptocurrency system created from a *hard fork* of Bitcoin (BTC), which took place on October 24, 2017 at block 491,407. The fork was initiated by a group of developers and investors dissatisfied with the direction Bitcoin had taken, in particular regarding the growing concentration of mining power in the hands of a few large farms using ASICs. Bitcoin Gold wanted to democratize the mining process by using a new proof-of-work algorithm, named *Equihash*, which is ASIC-resistant and therefore favors mining with graphics cards (GPUs). The goal was to make participation in mining accessible to more people in order to decentralize it and reduce the risks linked to centralization. BTG initially used the same mining algorithm as Zcash (ZEC), namely Equihash with the parameters (200,9). In June 2018, they modified it to adopt Equihash-BTG, a variant with the parameters (144,5), in order to strengthen ASIC resistance.

*Note that the altcoin Bitcoin Gold (BTG) should not be confused with bit gold, Nick Szabo's concept.*

entries.title: BTKN
entries.body: Token standard (*tokens*) native to the Spark protocol, allowing the issuance and management of digital assets directly on a layer above Bitcoin. BTKNs can represent stablecoins, loyalty tokens, reward points or any other tokenized asset. Unlike token protocols on other blockchains, BTKNs do not require smart contracts or complex deployment: the issuer uses the Spark SDK to create a token, issue its supply and carry out transfers.

entries.title: BTRUST
entries.body: Non-profit organization founded in February 2021 by Jack Dorsey and Jay-Z with an initial endowment of 500 bitcoins. Btrust's mission is to decentralize the development of Bitcoin software by encouraging and funding developers in countries of the Global South, notably in Africa and India. The organization offers training programs, development fellowships and grants to strengthen the contribution of these regions to Bitcoin's open-source code and its technical ecosystem.

entries.title: BUCKETING
entries.body:
Method of distributing peer addresses across the tables of Bitcoin Core's addrman module. Each address is assigned to a bucket ("bucket") by a hash computation that combines the address itself, the network group it comes from and a 256-bit secret key (`nKey`) specific to each node. This placement, deterministic but unpredictable from the outside, aims to prevent an attacker from predicting or controlling which positions they occupy in the tables.

The "new" and "tried" tables use distinct bucketing schemes. In the "new" table, the bucket depends on the source network group and the network group of the address. In the "tried" table, it depends only on the network group of the address itself. This separation of criteria limits an attacker's ability to monopolize buckets from a single source, which constitutes a defense against eclipse attacks.

entries.title: BULL BITCOIN
entries.body:
Canadian bitcoin exchange platform founded by Francis Pouliot. Bull Bitcoin stands out for its *non-custodial* model: unlike traditional exchange platforms, it does not take custody of its customers' bitcoins. Purchases are sent directly to the user's personal wallet, and sales are made from that same wallet.

The company adopts a strictly "Bitcoin only" philosophy and offers no other cryptocurrency. Bull Bitcoin supports payments via the Lightning Network for small-amount transactions. The platform is particularly popular in Canada and has expanded to other markets. Its *non-custodial* model reduces counterparty risk for users, since the platform never holds the funds, which brings it closer to the principles of financial sovereignty promoted by Bitcoin.

entries.title: BULL MARKET
entries.body: Prolonged period during which the price of an asset, such as bitcoin, rises relative to a fiat currency, typically the US dollar. The expression "Bull Run", in a more colloquial register, is often used to refer to this same phenomenon.

entries.title: BULL RUN
entries.body: Prolonged period during which the price of an asset, such as bitcoin, increases relative to a fiat currency, most often the US dollar. The expression "Bull Run" refers to the same phenomenon as "Bull Market", but in a more colloquial register.

entries.title: BULLETPROOFS
entries.body:
Zero-knowledge proof system (*zero-knowledge proofs*) used notably in *Confidential Transactions* to verify that an amount committed in a transaction lies within a valid range, without revealing its value. Bulletproofs were introduced in 2017 by Bünz, Bootle, Boneh, Poelstra, Wuille and Maxwell. They replace earlier range proofs (*Borromean ring signatures*) by producing significantly more compact proofs, whose size grows logarithmically (`O(\log n)`) with respect to the number of bits representing the value.

An evolution named Bulletproofs++, proposed by Liam Eagen, Sanket Kanjalkar, Tim Ruffing and Jonas Nick, further improves efficiency in terms of generation and verification. On Liquid, the adoption of Bulletproofs made it possible to reduce the size of confidential transactions, thereby lowering fees and slowing the growth of the chain.

entries.title: BURN ADDRESS
entries.body:
Bitcoin address to which funds are sent irreversibly, with no possibility of spending them afterward. No one possesses the corresponding private key: sending bitcoins to such an address amounts to destroying them permanently, unless it one day becomes possible to break the underlying cryptography.

These addresses are generally constructed arbitrarily, without being derived from a private key, so that one can prove one does not know it. The probability that a valid private key corresponds to a randomly chosen address is astronomically low, which makes the funds effectively unrecoverable. For example, there is the address: `1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE`.

Burning bitcoins can serve various purposes. The Counterparty protocol used it in 2014 during its *proof of burn* phase to distribute its own tokens in exchange for destroyed bitcoins. It can also be proof of irreversible commitment in certain cryptographic mechanisms, or simply a playful action.

entries.title: BUSINESS LOGIC
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Business Logic* encompasses all the internal rules and operations of a contract, described by its schema (that is, the very structure of the contract). It dictates how the contract's state can evolve and under what conditions.
